articles.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
articles.summaryB1: Poland has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz, a famous resistance fighter who used the codename 'Rój', which means 'Swarm' in Polish. He was a soldier who refused to stop fighting even after World War II ended in 1945. At that time, communist forces took control of Poland, and Dziemieszkiewicz believed this was wrong. He led a small armed unit in the forests and continued to resist the new government for many years. Fighters like him are known in Poland as the 'Cursed Soldiers' because they were loyal to their country but were hunted down and treated as criminals by the communist authorities. Dziemieszkiewicz was eventually captured and executed in 1951. His body was hidden in an unmarked grave, as was common with political prisoners at the time. For decades, his family and supporters did not know where he was buried. Scientists and historians worked together to identify his remains using modern methods. The discovery is a moment of recognition for Dziemieszkiewicz and others like him. Many Polish people feel it is right to honour these fighters and give them a proper burial. This kind of identification helps families find peace and keeps the memory of resistance fighters alive for future generations.

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it matters to find and honour resistance fighters like Dziemieszkiewicz, even many decades after their death?
articles.summaryB2: Polish authorities have successfully identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz, codenamed 'Rój' ('Swarm'), one of the most celebrated figures among Poland's post-war anti-communist underground. Dziemieszkiewicz commanded an armed partisan unit that continued fighting long after the formal conclusion of World War II, refusing to accept the communist regime that had seized control of the country with Soviet backing. His story is part of a larger phenomenon in Polish history: the so-called 'Cursed Soldiers', fighters who waged a guerrilla campaign against the communist state throughout the late 1940s and into the 1950s. The authorities systematically persecuted these men, and Dziemieszkiewicz was eventually captured and executed in 1951. His body was disposed of in a clandestine burial site, a deliberate attempt to erase both his physical remains and his legacy from public memory. The identification was made possible through forensic analysis, a process that has become a tool of historical reckoning in post-communist Poland. For decades, the communist state had sought to suppress the memory of such fighters, branding them as bandits rather than patriots. Since 1989, successive Polish governments have worked to rehabilitate their reputations. The discovery of Dziemieszkiewicz's remains is seen by many as an act of posthumous justice, restoring dignity to a man who was condemned precisely because he refused to submit to an illegitimate authority.

vocabularyB2.definition: A member of an armed group fighting unofficially against an occupying or oppressive force

A time when past actions, mistakes, or injustices are finally judged or addressed

articles.questionB2: In what ways does the forensic reckoning with figures like Dziemieszkiewicz reflect the difficulties post-communist societies face when trying to rehabilitate those persecuted by former regimes?

articles.title: Poland bans chaining of dogs and cats
articles.summaryB1:
Poland has passed a new law that bans keeping dogs and cats on chains. The president, Karol Nawrocki, signed the law after first refusing to accept an earlier version of it. He had vetoed that version, which means he sent it back to parliament without approving it. Parliament then made changes to the bill, and Nawrocki agreed to sign the revised version.

Before this law, it was common in Poland for dogs to be tied up outside on a chain, sometimes for many hours or even all day. Animal welfare groups had campaigned for a ban for a long time, saying that chaining animals causes them stress and suffering. Under the new rules, owners who chain their pets can face a penalty, such as a fine.

The law is part of a wider effort in Poland to improve how animals are treated. Many people believe that keeping a dog on a chain prevents it from moving freely and living a normal life. Supporters of the ban say it is a step forward for animal rights in the country.

Not everyone agrees, however. Some people in rural areas say that chaining dogs is a traditional practice and that the new rules are unfair. Despite this opposition, the law has now been approved and will come into force in Poland.

vocabularyB1.definition: When a leader officially refuses to approve a law, stopping it from passing.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a penalty is the best way to stop people from chaining animals, or are there better solutions?
articles.summaryB2:
Poland has enacted legislation banning the chaining of dogs and cats, marking a notable shift in the country's approach to animal protection. President Karol Nawrocki initially withheld his assent from an earlier draft of the bill, exercising his presidential veto and returning it to parliament for reconsideration. Lawmakers subsequently amended the text, and Nawrocki ultimately signed the revised legislation into law.

The practice of keeping dogs permanently or semi-permanently restrained on chains has long been prevalent in Poland, particularly in rural communities where dogs are traditionally kept as guard animals. Animal rights advocates had lobbied for an outright prohibition for years, arguing that prolonged chaining inflicts both physical and psychological harm on animals, severely restricting their freedom of movement and natural behaviour.

The new law introduces penalties for owners found to be in breach of the regulations, though critics from agricultural and rural communities contend that the legislation fails to account for the realities of farming life and represents an overreach by urban policymakers.

The reform reflects a gradual tightening of animal welfare standards across Europe, with several neighbouring countries having introduced similar restrictions in recent years. Proponents argue that the ban brings Poland in line with evolving ethical standards regarding the treatment of companion animals. Detractors, however, question whether enforcement will prove effective given the scale of the practice across the country's rural regions.

articles.questionB2: Given the tension between proponents of the ban and its detractors in rural communities, how should governments balance animal welfare legislation with deeply rooted cultural and practical traditions?

articles.title: Investors cool on Europe’s old-style defence firms
articles.summaryB1:
European defence companies have been struggling to attract investors. For many years, these firms made weapons and military equipment for governments. But now, investors are becoming less interested in supporting them. There are several reasons for this.

First, many of these companies face supply-chain problems. This means they cannot always get the parts and materials they need to build their equipment on time. Second, governments in Europe often make the process of buying military equipment very slow and complicated. These procurement obstacles make it hard for companies to earn money quickly.

Third, and perhaps most interesting, is the rise of drone warfare. Modern conflicts now use drones — small flying machines — more and more. Drones are cheaper and faster to produce than traditional weapons like tanks or fighter jets. Old-style defence firms are not well prepared to compete in this new area.

As a result, investors worry that these traditional companies may not grow as fast as newer, more modern defence businesses. Money is starting to move away from Europe's established defence giants toward smaller, more innovative companies.

This matters because Europe is currently trying to spend more on its own defence. If investors do not support the traditional firms, it could slow down Europe's efforts to build a stronger military. The future of European defence may depend on companies that are ready to change.

vocabularyB1.definition: The system of people and companies that provide parts and materials needed to make a product

articles.questionB1: Why might investors prefer to support innovative drone companies rather than traditional defence firms? What risks do old-style companies face?
articles.summaryB2:
Europe's established defence companies are losing their appeal among investors, as a combination of structural inefficiencies, bureaucratic procurement systems and the rapid rise of drone warfare reshapes the military industry.

For decades, Europe's legacy defence contractors — manufacturers of tanks, warships and fighter aircraft — enjoyed stable government contracts and steady revenues. However, investor sentiment has shifted noticeably. Supply-chain snags continue to delay production, raising doubts about delivery timelines and profitability. Meanwhile, the labyrinthine procurement processes that govern European military spending make it difficult for firms to translate political commitments into actual revenue streams in a timely fashion.

Perhaps most disruptive is the emergence of drone warfare as a dominant feature of modern conflict, most visibly demonstrated in Ukraine. Drones are relatively inexpensive, quick to manufacture and devastatingly effective — qualities that stand in sharp contrast to the costly and time-consuming products that old-style manufacturers specialise in. Investors are increasingly directing capital toward agile technology-focused start-ups better positioned to capitalise on this shift, rather than towards the incumbents.

This cooling of investor enthusiasm carries broader consequences at a particularly sensitive moment. European governments are under pressure to bolster their defence capabilities independently of the United States, yet the traditional industrial base that would underpin such ambitions is struggling to secure private funding.

The divergence between political urgency and investor caution highlights a structural tension: Europe wants to rearm swiftly, but the companies historically tasked with that mission may no longer be seen as the right vehicles for the job.

articles.questionB2: Given the divergence between Europe's political ambitions and investor caution toward incumbents, what structural reforms might encourage private capital to support the continent's rearmament goals?

articles.title: Dismissing Europe as a museum is glib. Think of it as a theme park
articles.summaryB1: Many people describe Europe as a 'museum' – a place full of old buildings and history, but not very modern or exciting. A new article in The Economist disagrees with this idea. It suggests a better way to think about Europe is as a 'theme park'. This might sound strange at first, but the comparison makes sense. A theme park is carefully designed to give visitors a strong experience. It looks after its attractions and makes sure people enjoy themselves. Europe does something similar. Its cities, traditions, and cultural heritage are not just old things people look at – they are actively maintained and presented to the world. The continent attracts hundreds of millions of tourists every year because it offers something unique: a living connection to history. The article argues that calling Europe a museum is too simple and even a little rude. Museums are passive places where things are kept behind glass. A theme park, on the other hand, is dynamic and engaging. Europe's culture is not frozen in time – it continues to grow and perform for the world. This reframing helps us appreciate Europe differently. Instead of seeing old culture as a weakness, we can see it as a strength that Europe has learned to share effectively with visitors from around the world.

vocabularyB1.definition: The traditions, buildings, and history passed down from previous generations.
To make people want to come to a place or be interested in something.

articles.questionB1: Do you think Europe's cultural heritage is a strength or a weakness in the modern world, and why does reframing it matter?
articles.summaryB2: The familiar jibe that Europe is a 'museum' – a repository of glorious but inert civilisation, more preoccupied with preserving the past than shaping the future – has long been a convenient shorthand for critics, particularly those in the United States and Asia who equate dynamism with novelty. A recent Economist article pushes back against this characterisation, proposing instead that Europe be understood as a theme park: a deliberate, meticulously curated experience designed to deliver cultural spectacle at scale. The distinction, while playful, carries genuine analytical weight. A museum is passive, detached, and curatorial in the coldest sense. A theme park, by contrast, is a performative enterprise – one that consciously stages its identity for an audience and derives economic value from doing so. Europe, the argument goes, has effectively commodified its history, turning centuries of architecture, ritual, and tradition into an immersive offering that draws hundreds of millions of visitors annually. Far from being a sign of stagnation, this capacity to package and export cultural experience represents a sophisticated form of soft power. The article implicitly challenges the assumption that economic vitality must come from technological disruption alone. Europe's model – heritage as spectacle, history as product – may be more strategically coherent than its detractors acknowledge. The theme park metaphor ultimately invites us to reassess what productivity and global influence can look like in the twenty-first century.

vocabularyB2.definition: A description or portrayal of something, often simplifying it for a particular effect.
Turned into something that can be sold or traded for economic gain.
A state of no growth, progress, or development; being stuck in place.
The ability to influence other countries through culture and attraction rather than military force.
People who criticise or speak negatively about something or someone.

articles.questionB2: If Europe has effectively commodified its history as the article suggests, does this transform soft power into a sustainable economic model, or does it risk hollowing out authentic cultural identity?

articles.title: America’s AI labs are under threat from cheap Chinese rivals
articles.summaryB1: American companies have led the world in building artificial intelligence (AI) for many years. Big names like OpenAI and Google have spent billions of dollars on powerful AI systems. However, Chinese AI companies are now offering strong competition. They are producing AI models that cost much less to build and use, and they are making these models available to everyone for free. This type of AI is called an open-weight model, which means anyone can download and use it without paying. Demand for these free models is growing very fast around the world. Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, have shown that you do not need to spend enormous amounts of money to create good AI. This is a serious challenge for American labs, which have built their business around selling expensive AI services. If customers can get similar results from a free Chinese model, they may stop paying for American products. This situation is making investors and governments in the United States worried. Some people think American companies need to change their strategy to stay competitive. Others believe that American AI is still better in certain areas. Either way, the rise of cheap Chinese AI is changing the technology industry in a big way, and the competition between the two countries is getting stronger every month.

vocabularyB1.definition: A situation where two or more people or groups try to be better than each other.
An AI system that anyone can download and use for free, without restrictions.
Very, very large in size or amount.
A plan that you use to achieve a goal, especially in business or games.
Able to succeed against others who are trying to do the same thing.

articles.questionB1: If a free Chinese AI model gives similar results to an expensive American one, what strategy should American companies use to stay competitive?
articles.summaryB2: For years, American AI laboratories such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind have dominated the global artificial intelligence industry, backed by colossal investment and the assumption that scale and spending would guarantee dominance. That assumption is now being tested by a wave of low-cost Chinese rivals offering open-weight models — AI systems whose parameters are publicly released, allowing anyone to download, modify, and deploy them at minimal expense. Demand for such models is soaring, as businesses and developers worldwide seek capable AI tools without the steep subscription fees charged by American providers. Chinese firms, most notably DeepSeek, have demonstrated that frontier-level AI performance need not require frontier-level expenditure, undermining a core premise of the American industry's pricing model. This has prompted a reassessment among investors, who had previously poured capital into US labs on the expectation of long-term profitability. The commercial viability of American AI giants now looks less certain, particularly if open-weight alternatives continue to close the performance gap. Geopolitical tensions add another dimension to the rivalry, with policymakers in Washington debating whether national security justifies further restricting Chinese access to advanced semiconductors. Meanwhile, some analysts argue that American labs retain an edge in proprietary, closed models tailored for enterprise clients. Nevertheless, the proliferation of high-quality, freely available Chinese AI is fundamentally reshaping the competitive dynamics of the global technology sector.

vocabularyB2.definition: Extremely large; far bigger than normal or expected.

The ability of a business or product to make enough money to survive long-term.
A rapid increase in the number or spread of something.
Owned exclusively by a company and not available for others to use freely.

articles.questionB2: Given the proliferation of high-quality open-weight models from China, can the commercial viability of American AI labs be sustained, and what structural changes might be necessary to ensure their survival?

articles.title: Berlin Pride attack suspect shot and killed during police operation
articles.summaryB1: A man named Abdul Ballout was shot and killed by police in Berlin, Germany. The incident happened in a western part of the city called a borough. Police say that Ballout rushed at officers carrying a knife, and they shot him in response. Ballout was a suspect in an earlier attack that took place during Berlin Pride, a large public event where people march to support LGBTQ+ rights. The attack at the Pride event shocked many people in the city. After the attack, police searched for Ballout and eventually found him. When officers approached him, he did not surrender. Instead, he charged at them with a knife, and they used lethal force to stop him. The death of a suspect during a police operation often raises questions about how such situations are handled. Some people want to know if there were other ways to stop him without shooting. Others believe that officers had no choice because their lives were in danger. Berlin Pride is a well-known annual event that attracts thousands of visitors. Violence at such events is rare but deeply troubling. German authorities are now investigating both the original attack and the police shooting to understand exactly what happened.

vocabularyB1.definition: An official district or area within a large city
A person believed to have committed a crime, but not yet proven guilty
To stop fighting and give yourself up to the police or enemy

articles.questionB1: Do you think police always have a choice when dealing with a dangerous suspect, or is lethal force sometimes unavoidable?
articles.summaryB2: German police shot and killed Abdul Ballout, the prime suspect in a knife attack carried out during Berlin Pride, after he lunged at officers with a blade during a police operation in a western borough of the German capital. According to authorities, officers were left with no alternative when Ballout advanced on them wielding a knife, forcing them to open fire. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Ballout had been sought in connection with the earlier assault at Berlin Pride, one of Europe's most prominent LGBTQ+ gatherings, which draws hundreds of thousands of participants annually. The attack on Pride marchers had already provoked widespread condemnation and heightened anxieties about the safety of LGBTQ+ spaces in Germany. The fatal outcome of the subsequent police operation is likely to intensify public debate about the use of force by law enforcement. Civil liberties advocates may scrutinise whether de-escalation tactics were adequately considered before officers resorted to shooting. German authorities, meanwhile, have confirmed that both the original assault and the circumstances surrounding the fatal shooting are now subject to formal investigation. The case reflects a tension that many democratic societies grapple with: balancing the protection of marginalised communities against the accountability of state institutions when deadly force is deployed. Berlin's police force has not yet issued a detailed statement outlining the full sequence of events.

vocabularyB2.definition: Made a sudden, aggressive forward movement towards someone
Holding and using a weapon or tool in a threatening or active way
Strong and official public criticism or disapproval of an action
The process of reducing tension or danger in a conflict to avoid violence

articles.questionB2: When a suspect is killed during a police operation, how should authorities scrutinise the use of de-escalation tactics to ensure both public safety and institutional accountability?

articles.title: Police and park rangers step up joint patrols in Poland’s Tatras after series of tourist offences
articles.summaryB1: Police and park rangers in the Tatra Mountains in southern Poland have started working together more often to watch over visitors. They are doing more joint patrols to stop tourists from breaking the rules of the national park. Authorities say that a number of offences have been recorded recently, including people bathing in mountain lakes. This is against the rules because it can harm the natural environment. The Tatras are home to a fragile ecosystem, which means the plants and animals there can be easily damaged by human activity. The lakes are especially sensitive, and even swimming can disturb the water and the wildlife that depends on it. Park rangers already patrol the area regularly, but police are now joining them to make enforcement stronger. Visitors who break the rules can face fines or other penalties. Officials want tourists to enjoy the mountains responsibly and to follow the regulations that protect the park. The Tatras are one of the most visited natural areas in Poland, and managing the pressure from large numbers of tourists is an ongoing challenge. By increasing patrols, authorities hope to reduce damage to the environment and remind visitors that the rules exist for a good reason.

vocabularyB1.definition: To walk around an area regularly to check that everything is safe and rules are followed
An action that breaks a rule or law

articles.questionB1: Do you think stronger enforcement and more patrols are the best way to protect a fragile natural area like the Tatras? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: Polish police and Tatra National Park rangers have intensified joint patrols following a series of violations by tourists, with authorities citing bathing in mountain lakes as among the most damaging transgressions. The move reflects growing institutional pressure to protect one of Central Europe's most ecologically sensitive alpine environments from the consequences of mass tourism. The Tatra Mountains attract millions of visitors each year, and their fragile ecosystems — encompassing rare flora, mountain streams, and glacial lakes — are particularly vulnerable to human interference. Bathing, though perhaps appearing harmless to the casual visitor, can introduce pollutants, disturb aquatic life, and erode the delicate balance of these water bodies. By deploying law enforcement officers alongside park rangers, the authorities are signalling a shift toward more assertive deterrence rather than relying solely on public awareness campaigns. Tourists found to be in violation of park regulations may face financial penalties. Officials have used the patrols as an opportunity to reiterate the rules to visitors and remind them that the restrictions are in place to safeguard biodiversity. The initiative also highlights a wider tension between the economic benefits of tourism and the need to preserve natural heritage. As visitor numbers show no sign of declining, co-ordinated responses between different state bodies may become a standard feature of national park management in Poland.

vocabularyB2.definition: Actions that break a rule or go beyond acceptable boundaries
The use of warnings or punishments to discourage people from doing something wrong
Confident and direct in taking action or expressing authority
The variety of different plants, animals, and other living things in a particular area
Acts of breaking a rule, law, or formal agreement

articles.questionB2: To what extent can deterrence through increased patrols and fines effectively protect biodiversity in heavily visited national parks, and what other approaches might be needed?

articles.title: EU clears $110bn Paramount and Warner Bros merger, but it remains on hold in US
articles.summaryB1:
The European Commission has approved a huge merger between two major American media companies: Paramount Global and Warner Bros. Discovery. Together, these companies are worth about 110 billion dollars. The deal would join two of the biggest entertainment studios in the world, creating a company that owns well-known brands like CNN, HBO, MTV, and Paramount Pictures.

The European Commission gave its approval, but it came with conditions. This means that Paramount must agree to certain rules before the merger can fully go ahead. These conditions are designed to protect competition in the media market and to make sure other companies can still compete fairly.

However, the merger is still on hold in the United States. American regulators have not yet given their approval, so the deal cannot be completed yet. Both companies are waiting for a decision from US authorities.

This merger matters because it could change the way people watch films and television. Large mergers like this one can reduce the number of choices available to viewers and affect the prices of streaming services. Critics worry that having fewer, bigger companies in the entertainment industry could be bad for consumers. Supporters, on the other hand, argue that a bigger combined company would be stronger and better able to compete with other streaming giants like Netflix.

vocabularyB1.definition: When two companies join together to become one new company
Official permission or agreement that something is allowed to happen
Rules or requirements that must be followed before something is allowed
Government officials or organisations that control how businesses operate
When companies try to win customers by offering better products or prices

articles.questionB1: Do you think regulators should set strict conditions when they give approval for large company mergers? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
The European Commission has granted regulatory approval for the proposed $110 billion merger between Paramount Global and Warner Bros. Discovery, two of Hollywood's most storied media conglomerates. The green light, however, came with stipulations attached specifically to Paramount, requiring the company to meet certain obligations designed to safeguard fair competition within the European media market.

The combined entity would bring together an extraordinary portfolio of assets, encompassing brands such as HBO, CNN, MTV, Paramount Pictures, and CBS, creating a media powerhouse with vast reach across both traditional broadcasting and streaming platforms. Proponents of the deal argue that consolidation of this scale is a necessary response to the dominance of streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon Prime, which have steadily eroded the market share of legacy media companies.

Despite the EU's conditional endorsement, the merger remains in limbo in the United States, where domestic regulators have yet to issue a ruling. The transatlantic gap in regulatory timelines reflects the differing pace and approach of American and European antitrust authorities.

The deal has drawn scrutiny from critics who warn that such sweeping consolidation could diminish consumer choice and reduce the diversity of voices in global media. The outcome of the US regulatory review is expected to be a defining factor in whether this landmark merger ultimately proceeds, making the coming months a period of considerable uncertainty for both companies and their investors.

vocabularyB2.definition: Specific conditions or requirements that must be met as part of an agreement
Very large companies made up of many different businesses or brands
The process of merging smaller companies into fewer, larger ones
In an uncertain situation where progress is paused and no decision has been made
Relating to laws that prevent companies from gaining too much market power unfairly

articles.questionB2: Given that consolidation of this scale may limit consumer choice, do antitrust authorities in different countries face conflicting pressures when evaluating cross-border media mergers?

articles.title: French politicians can’t get enough of ‘De Gaulle’
articles.summaryB1: A new French film about Charles de Gaulle has become very popular among French politicians. The film is five hours long and tells the story of one of France's most famous leaders. De Gaulle was a general and later the president of France. He is remembered for leading France during difficult times, including World War Two and a period of great political change in the 1960s. Many French people still admire him deeply today. The film has captured the attention of politicians because France will have a presidential election next year. Politicians from different parties are watching the film and talking about it openly. Some seem to use de Gaulle's image and ideas to inspire their own campaigns. The film shows the spirit of the times in French politics right now. People are thinking about leadership, national identity, and what it means to be a strong leader. The word zeitgeist describes this shared feeling or mood of a particular moment in history. The film seems to reflect what many French voters care about as the election approaches. It is a reminder that history and politics are closely connected in France. De Gaulle remains a powerful symbol, and this film has brought his legacy back into everyday political conversation.

vocabularyB1.definition: To respect and have a very positive opinion of someone or something
To make people notice and become interested in something
The lasting impact or influence a person leaves after their life or work

articles.questionB1: What does it tell us about French identity today that so many politicians admire a historical leader like de Gaulle?
articles.summaryB2: A sweeping five-hour cinematic portrait of Charles de Gaulle has taken French political circles by storm, arriving at a moment when the country is gearing up for next year's presidential election. The film chronicles the life of France's towering wartime leader and founding father of the Fifth Republic, a figure whose shadow looms large over French political culture to this day. What is striking is not merely the film's artistic ambition but the enthusiasm with which politicians across the spectrum have embraced it. In an era of fragmented parties and polarised electorates, de Gaulle appears to offer something rare: a unifying myth of strong, visionary leadership. The film has been widely described as capturing the zeitgeist of contemporary French politics, reflecting a collective longing for decisive authority at a time of institutional uncertainty. Critics and commentators have noted that politicians invoking de Gaulle's image risk projecting nostalgia rather than genuine vision, effectively using history as a rhetorical prop. Nevertheless, the film's resonance suggests that de Gaulle's model of leadership — assertive, independent, and unapologetically nationalist — retains its appeal across generations. With the presidential race on the horizon, the timing of the film's release feels anything but accidental. It has reignited a long-running debate about what kind of leader France needs, and whether the answer, once again, lies buried in its past.

Something used in speech or argument to persuade people rather than for genuine reasons

articles.questionB2: When politicians are invoking a historical figure like de Gaulle during an election campaign, how can voters distinguish between genuine political vision and mere rhetorical prop?

articles.title: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
articles.summaryB1:
In 2023, someone hacked into OpenAI, the company that makes ChatGPT, and stole information about how their AI systems work. OpenAI told its employees about the hack but decided not to make it public. The company said no customer data was taken, so they did not think it was a serious threat. However, some people inside OpenAI were worried. They felt the company was not being careful enough about security risks, especially the danger that AI technology could fall into the wrong hands.

The AI research company Hugging Face later looked at the hack and said something surprising. They believed the attack was carried out at superhuman speed, meaning it happened much faster than a normal person could work. This suggests that an AI system may have guided the hack with little or no human involvement.

This raises a big question: are AI companies doing enough to protect their systems? Some experts think the hack was a warning shot — a sign that bigger attacks could happen in the future. Others believe it was more of a publicity stunt, designed to get attention rather than cause real damage. Either way, many people now think AI companies need stronger security measures. The debate continues about how much danger these kinds of cyber attacks really pose to the public.

vocabularyB1.definition: An illegal attempt to access a computer system or steal digital information
Something that could cause harm or danger in the future
Far beyond what a normal human being is able to do
An action meant to signal that something more serious could happen later
Something done mainly to attract attention, not for a serious purpose

articles.questionB1: Do you think the hack on OpenAI was a genuine warning shot or just a publicity stunt — and why does your answer matter?
articles.summaryB2:
In 2023, OpenAI — the organisation behind ChatGPT — suffered a security breach in which an attacker gained access to internal communications and extracted details about the company's AI research. OpenAI disclosed the incident to staff but chose not to inform the public, reasoning that no customer data had been compromised and that the perpetrator appeared to be an individual with no known ties to a foreign government. The decision to stay silent, however, troubled some employees who felt it reflected a dangerously complacent attitude toward AI-related security vulnerabilities.

The incident has since attracted renewed scrutiny following an analysis by Hugging Face, a prominent AI research company. Their investigators concluded that the breach was executed at superhuman speed, implying that an AI system — operating with minimal or no human oversight — may have been the driving force behind the attack. If accurate, this would mark a troubling precedent: an AI being used as a tool to compromise another AI organisation.

Opinion remains divided on how to interpret the episode. Sceptics argue it amounts to little more than a publicity stunt, inflated by media coverage to generate alarm disproportionate to the actual damage caused. Others, however, contend that dismissing it so readily would be a mistake, and that the incident exposes genuine gaps in how AI companies handle cybersecurity. As AI systems grow more capable, the question of who bears responsibility for safeguarding them is becoming harder to ignore.

articles.questionB2: Given that the breach may have been executed with minimal human oversight, what does this precedent suggest about the responsibilities AI companies have toward the public and governments in disclosing security incidents?

articles.title: Trump reopens the tariff fight
articles.summaryB1: Iceland is holding a vote to decide whether to restart talks about joining the European Union. This is a big decision for the country. Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009 but stopped the process in 2013. Now, people are thinking about it again. Many Icelanders are worried about security in Europe, especially because of the war in Ukraine. There is also economic uncertainty, which means people are not sure what will happen to prices and jobs in the future. One of the main problems is fishing. Iceland's fishing industry is very important to its economy, and many people do not want the EU to control their fishing waters. At the same time, there is another story connected to the EU. Donald Trump has threatened to introduce new tariffs on European goods. This happened after the EU fined Google 890 million euros for breaking competition rules. Trump said the fine was unfair to an American company. Tariffs are taxes that make imported goods more expensive. If the US adds tariffs to European products, it could hurt businesses and trade on both sides. These two stories show that the EU is dealing with difficult questions both inside Europe and in its relationship with the United States.

vocabularyB1.definition: The process of officially joining an organisation or group, like the EU.

Laws that make sure companies behave fairly and do not control a market unfairly.

articles.questionB1: If Iceland joins the EU, do you think it should accept EU competition rules even if they affect its most important industries, like fishing?
articles.summaryB2:
Iceland has reopened a long-dormant debate about EU membership, with citizens casting votes on whether to resume accession talks that were suspended over a decade ago. The referendum reflects a confluence of pressures: heightened security anxieties following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, economic headwinds, and — perhaps most contentiously — the question of sovereignty over Iceland's fishing waters. Fishing is not merely an industry in Iceland; it is a deeply ingrained part of national identity, and many citizens remain deeply opposed to ceding control of those waters to Brussels.

Meanwhile, transatlantic trade tensions have flared once again. Donald Trump has threatened to impose sweeping new tariffs on European goods in retaliation for the EU's decision to fine Google €890 million for violations of its antitrust framework. Trump characterised the penalty as an attack on American business interests, framing it as part of a pattern of European overreach. This posture signals a willingness to weaponise trade policy in defence of US tech giants, regardless of the legal merits of the EU ruling.

Together, these two developments illustrate the competing pressures bearing down on the EU. It must simultaneously manage the expectations of potential new members who harbour genuine reservations about deeper integration, while defending its regulatory authority against external pushback from Washington. The EU's capacity to hold firm on both fronts will shape its credibility as a geopolitical actor in the months ahead.

vocabularyB2.definition: Not active for a period of time, but capable of becoming active again.
A coming together of several different things or influences at the same time.
A set of laws designed to prevent companies from gaining unfair monopoly power.
Going beyond acceptable or legal limits of power or authority.
Doubts or concerns that stop someone from fully agreeing with something.

articles.questionB2: Given Iceland's reservations about fishing sovereignty and Trump's use of tariffs as political retaliation, how effectively can the EU assert its regulatory authority without deepening divisions both internally and with Washington?

articles.title: Extension du marché carbone : le jour où Macron et Bayrou ont dit non à quatre ministres
articles.summaryB1: In May 2025, four French government ministers wrote a letter to President Macron and Prime Minister Bayrou. They wanted France to quickly introduce a second carbon market. A carbon market is a system where companies must pay for the pollution they produce. The ministers believed this would generate revenue — money collected by the government — that could help France reduce its carbon emissions. They argued that France needed to act fast to fund its plans to become cleaner and greener. However, both Macron and Bayrou rejected the proposal. The ministers did not succeed in convincing the top leaders. The letter was not made public at the time, but the news website Politico obtained and revealed it. This story shows that even within the French government, there are disagreements about environmental policy. Some ministers are pushing for stronger action on climate change, while the president and prime minister are more cautious. Carbon markets already exist in Europe, but a second one would cover more sectors of the economy. The debate over how to fund the transition away from fossil fuels is ongoing in France, as in many other countries. This internal conflict highlights how difficult it can be to agree on climate policy.

vocabularyB1.definition: A system where companies buy and sell the right to produce pollution.
To produce or bring in money, usually for a government or organisation.
Gases, especially harmful ones, released into the air by machines or industry.
A formal plan or suggestion that someone puts forward for others to consider.
Careful and not wanting to take risks or make quick decisions.

articles.questionB1: Do you think governments should use a carbon market to generate revenue for protecting the environment? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: A confidential letter obtained by Politico has shed light on a little-known internal dispute within the French government. In May 2025, four ministers jointly lobbied the Élysée and Matignon — the offices of President Macron and Prime Minister Bayrou respectively — urging them to swiftly implement a second carbon market. Their pitch centred on the need to mobilise funds for decarbonisation efforts at speed, arguing that extending the existing carbon pricing mechanism would unlock a new stream of public finance for France's green transition. Both Macron and Bayrou refused, leaving the ministers' push effectively dead in the water. The revelation raises questions about the coherence of France's climate strategy at the highest levels of government. Carbon markets function by assigning a financial cost to greenhouse gas emissions, incentivising companies to reduce their environmental footprint. A second such mechanism, as the ministers envisaged, would have extended this approach to additional economic sectors not yet covered by existing EU schemes. The episode illustrates a recurring tension in climate governance: the ambition of those advocating for accelerated action versus the restraint exercised by political leaders wary of economic or political backlash. That four ministers felt compelled to write formally to the president suggests the disagreement was more than a routine policy skirmish — it points to a deeper rift over how aggressively France should pursue its decarbonisation agenda.

vocabularyB2.definition: Tried to persuade someone in power to support a particular policy or decision.
The process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions from an economy or sector.
The quality of being logical, consistent, and well-organised as a whole.

A serious disagreement that divides people or groups who were previously aligned.

articles.questionB2: Given the rift between the four ministers and France's top leadership over decarbonisation funding, what does this episode reveal about the structural challenges of translating climate ambition into coherent government policy?

articles.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
articles.summaryB1: Poland and Ukraine have a painful shared history. During World War Two, Ukrainian nationalist groups killed tens of thousands of Polish civilians in what is now known as the Volhynia massacre. This happened mainly in 1943 and 1944, and it has caused tension between the two countries for many years. Now, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has presented a five-point plan to help resolve this long-standing dispute. Poland has welcomed the proposal. One of the main promises in the plan is that Ukraine will open its historical archives. This means researchers and families will be able to access old documents and records about the killings. Ukraine has also pledged to allow more exhumations to take place. Exhumations involve digging up the remains of victims so they can be identified and given a proper burial. For many Polish families, finding the remains of their relatives is extremely meaningful. The plan is seen as a positive step forward in repairing relations between the two neighbouring countries. Poland and Ukraine have generally been close allies since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, the unresolved issue of the wartime massacres has sometimes created difficulties. Both governments now appear committed to working together to address this sensitive part of their shared past.

vocabularyB1.definition: To find a solution to a problem or disagreement
A serious disagreement between two people, groups, or countries
A collection of historical documents and records kept for reference
The act of digging up a dead body from the ground

articles.questionB1: Why do you think allowing exhumations and opening archives might help resolve a painful dispute between two countries?
articles.summaryB2: Poland has responded positively to a five-point plan put forward by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky aimed at settling one of the most fraught chapters in Polish-Ukrainian relations: the Volhynia massacres of 1943–44, in which Ukrainian nationalist forces killed an estimated 100,000 Polish civilians. The killings have long been a source of historical grievance between the two nations, periodically straining diplomatic ties even as Warsaw and Kyiv have maintained a largely cooperative relationship since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. Among the concrete commitments outlined in Zelensky's proposal, Ukraine has pledged to open its historical archives and to permit a greater number of exhumations of massacre victims. Access to archival materials is seen as indispensable for historians and forensic investigators seeking to establish a more complete account of events, while exhumations offer bereaved Polish families the possibility of recovering and properly burying the remains of relatives killed decades ago. Polish officials have welcomed the plan as a tangible gesture of goodwill, though analysts caution that translating such pledges into verifiable action will require sustained political will on both sides. The initiative comes at a delicate moment, with Poland playing a central role in supporting Ukraine militarily and diplomatically amid the ongoing war with Russia. Reconciliation over wartime atrocities is widely regarded as a prerequisite for deepening the two countries' long-term partnership.

vocabularyB2.definition: Full of difficulties, tension, or negative emotions

articles.questionB2: To what extent can opening archives and permitting exhumations genuinely address deep historical grievances, and what further steps might be needed to achieve lasting reconciliation over wartime atrocities?

articles.title: Europe’s public broadcasters go from prime time to hard-to-find
articles.summaryB1: Public broadcasters in Europe are losing viewers and facing serious problems. These are television and radio channels that governments fund to provide news, culture, and entertainment for everyone. For many years, they were the most popular channels in their countries. Now, fewer people are watching them, especially young people. Teenagers and young adults prefer streaming services like Netflix or YouTube. They find public TV old-fashioned and boring. This means public broadcasters are getting less funding because governments see fewer reasons to support them. At the same time, some politicians are attacking these channels, saying they are biased or too expensive. These critics want to cut their budgets or even close them. Public broadcasters also struggle to compete with big international companies that have much more money to spend on programmes. Some channels are trying to change by making apps and online content, but it is difficult to attract young audiences who grew up with social media. The situation is serious because public broadcasters were designed to inform citizens and support local culture. If they disappear or become very weak, people may get their news only from private companies or social media. Many experts say this could damage democracy, because good public media helps people stay informed and make better decisions.

vocabularyB1.definition: Money given by a government or organisation to pay for something

To try to be more successful than others doing the same thing
To make someone interested in or want to come to something

articles.questionB1: Why is it so difficult for public broadcasters to attract young audiences, and does this matter for democracy?
articles.summaryB2: Europe's public broadcasters, long regarded as the bedrock of national media ecosystems, are confronting an existential crisis driven by two converging forces: generational indifference and political hostility. Institutions such as the BBC, France Télévisions, and their counterparts across the continent built their reputations on universal reach and editorial independence. Today, that legacy is under threat. Younger audiences have largely defected to streaming platforms and social media, leaving public broadcasters with ageing viewership and dwindling relevance in prime-time schedules. The resulting decline in audiences weakens the political case for sustaining generous licence fees or state subsidies, creating a vicious cycle of reduced budgets and diminished output quality. Compounding this financial strain is a wave of ideological attacks from populist politicians, who routinely characterise public media as elitist or politically slanted, using culture-war rhetoric to justify budget cuts or editorial interference. Attempts to adapt — through streaming apps, social media presence, and youth-oriented content — have met with mixed results, as public broadcasters lack the financial firepower of global platforms. The stakes extend well beyond institutional survival. Public broadcasters have traditionally served as a bulwark against misinformation and a guarantor of pluralism in national debates. Their weakening risks leaving citizens more dependent on algorithmically curated feeds and commercially driven outlets, with potentially corrosive effects on informed civic participation across Europe.

vocabularyB2.definition: The solid foundation or most basic and reliable part of something

Keeping something going or supporting it over a long period of time
To describe something or someone in a particular way, often to influence opinion
Something that protects against danger or unwanted change; a strong defence

articles.questionB2: If public broadcasters have historically served as a bulwark against misinformation, how should governments and societies respond when sustaining them becomes both financially and politically contentious?

articles.title: Poland begins construction of €2.3bn deepwater port on Baltic coast
articles.summaryB1: Poland has started building a large new deepwater port on its Baltic Sea coast. The project costs around 2.3 billion euros, making it one of the biggest infrastructure investments in the country's recent history. A deepwater port can handle very large ships that cannot enter smaller, shallower harbours. Construction has now officially begun, and the terminal is expected to be finished in the coming years. The port will not only serve Poland but also its landlocked neighbours – the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Austria, and Hungary. These countries have no access to the sea, so they depend on other nations to import and export goods by ship. Having a nearby terminal on the Baltic coast will make trade cheaper and faster for all of them. For Poland, the port will help boost its economy and strengthen its position as a major trade hub in Central Europe. The project also supports efforts to reduce dependence on more distant ports in Western Europe. Overall, this new terminal could change how goods move across the region and bring economic benefits to several countries at the same time.

vocabularyB1.definition: A harbour deep enough for very large ships to enter and dock safely
Surrounded by land on all sides, with no access to the sea
Basic systems and structures a country needs, like roads, ports, and bridges

articles.questionB1: Poland's new deepwater port will serve landlocked countries like Hungary and Slovakia. Do you think sharing infrastructure between neighbours is a good idea? Why?
articles.summaryB2: Poland has officially broken ground on a major new deepwater port along its Baltic coastline, with total investment projected at approximately 2.3 billion euros. The development marks one of the most ambitious maritime infrastructure undertakings in the country's post-communist era and reflects Warsaw's ambitions to position itself as a dominant logistics player in Central Europe. The terminal is designed to accommodate large-capacity vessels that exceed the draught limitations of existing Polish ports, opening new possibilities for high-volume seaborne trade. What distinguishes this project from similar regional developments is its explicitly multinational scope. The facility is intended to serve not only domestic freight needs but also to provide sea access for four landlocked neighbours – the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Austria, and Hungary – none of which has direct coastline. For these countries, gaining reliable proximity to a deep-sea terminal could substantially reduce transit costs and ease supply chain dependencies on ports in Hamburg, Trieste, or Rotterdam. From a geopolitical standpoint, the port may also reinforce Poland's strategic role within the European Union's internal market by diversifying trade corridors away from Western European gateways. Critics may question whether projected freight volumes justify the expenditure, but proponents argue that long-term regional integration makes the investment commercially sound. Construction timelines have not yet been fully disclosed, though the project is expected to reshape cargo flows across Central Europe for decades to come.

articles.questionB2: Given that the new terminal aims to redirect seaborne trade away from established Western European gateways, how might this shift in trade corridors affect the economic and political balance within the EU?

articles.title: Demis Hassabis has a plan to harness AI safely
articles.summaryB1:
Demis Hassabis is one of the most powerful people in artificial intelligence. He co-founded Google DeepMind, one of the world's leading AI research companies. In a recent exclusive interview with The Economist, he shared his vision for the future of AI and explained how he believes it can be developed safely.

AI is becoming more advanced every year. Many people worry that it could become dangerous if it is not controlled properly. Hassabis understands these concerns. He believes that scientists and companies must work carefully to make sure AI benefits humanity rather than causing harm.

His plan focuses on responsible development. This means testing AI systems thoroughly before releasing them to the public. It also means being transparent about how these systems work and what their limitations are. Hassabis thinks that safety and progress do not have to be in conflict with each other.

Google DeepMind has already made remarkable achievements in science, including using AI to solve problems in biology and medicine. Hassabis wants to continue this work while keeping safety at the centre of everything the company does.

This interview matters because Hassabis is not just a researcher — he is a decision-maker at one of the most powerful technology companies in the world. His approach to AI could influence how the entire industry develops in the coming years.

vocabularyB1.definition: Started a company or organisation together with one or more other people
A conversation given to only one journalist or publication, not shared with others
A clear idea or plan about what the future should look like
Open and honest, not hiding information from others
Surprising and impressive in a very positive way

articles.questionB1: Do you think it is possible to have a clear vision for making AI safe while still allowing it to develop quickly? Why?
articles.summaryB2:
Demis Hassabis, the co-founder of Google DeepMind and one of the most influential figures in artificial intelligence, has outlined his strategy for developing AI responsibly in an exclusive interview with The Economist. His intervention comes at a moment when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny from governments, researchers, and the public alike.

Hassabis argues that safety and scientific ambition are not mutually exclusive. Rather than treating caution as an obstacle to progress, he advocates for embedding safety considerations directly into the research process from the outset. This stance puts him at the intersection of two camps that often appear opposed: those who want to accelerate AI development and those who urge restraint.

Under his stewardship, Google DeepMind has achieved notable breakthroughs in scientific domains, particularly in structural biology, where AI has been used to predict protein structures with extraordinary accuracy. Hassabis sees this as a blueprint for how AI can be deployed to address some of humanity's most pressing challenges without compromising ethical standards.

His broader argument rests on the idea that the most capable AI systems must also be the most accountable. He calls for greater transparency from developers and more rigorous testing before new systems reach the public. Critics might question whether a company with significant commercial interests can truly self-regulate, but Hassabis insists that long-term trust depends on demonstrating restraint as much as capability.

His vision could shape industry norms for years to come.

Describes two things that cannot both be true or happen at the same time
The responsible management and care of something on behalf of others
A detailed plan or model that others can follow to achieve something
To control your own behaviour or industry without needing outside rules or enforcement

articles.questionB2: Given that Google DeepMind operates under significant commercial pressures, how convincing is Hassabis's case that a company can genuinely self-regulate AI development without independent oversight?

articles.title: Volkswagen hires 100 sheep to cut grass at Polish solar farm as experiment in agrivoltaics
articles.summaryB1:
Volkswagen, the German car company, has started an unusual experiment at a solar farm in Poland. Instead of using machines to cut the grass, they have hired 100 sheep to do the job. The sheep will eat the grass growing between and under the solar panels, keeping the area tidy and clean.

The project is being run together with a local university. It is part of research into agrivoltaics, which means using the same piece of land for both farming and generating solar energy at the same time. This idea is becoming more popular around the world because it allows farmers and energy companies to share land more efficiently.

Sheep are a good choice for this kind of work because they are small enough to move safely around the solar panels without damaging them. They do not need fuel or electricity to operate, and they also produce natural fertiliser for the soil.

For Volkswagen, this experiment shows that a car manufacturer can also be interested in sustainable farming practices. The company wants to reduce its impact on the environment, and this project is one way to experiment with greener methods.

The results of the research will help scientists and businesses understand whether combining agriculture with solar energy production is truly practical on a larger scale. Poland, which has been expanding its solar energy capacity, could benefit a great deal from such findings.

vocabularyB1.definition: Flat devices that collect sunlight and turn it into electricity
A substance added to soil to help plants grow better
A company that makes products in large quantities in a factory
Done in a way that does not damage the environment long term
The maximum amount of something that a system can produce or hold

articles.questionB1: Do you think using sheep instead of machines at solar farms is a sustainable idea? What other animals or natural methods could be useful?
articles.summaryB2:
Volkswagen has launched an experiment at a solar farm in Poland, deploying 100 sheep to manage vegetation between the panels rather than relying on conventional mechanical mowing. The initiative, carried out in collaboration with a local university, serves a dual purpose: it keeps the site maintained while contributing to academic research on agrivoltaics, a discipline that explores the co-location of agricultural activity and photovoltaic energy generation on the same plot of land.

Agrivoltaics has been gaining traction globally as land scarcity and the rapid expansion of renewable energy infrastructure push developers to find more efficient uses of available terrain. By integrating livestock grazing into solar farm management, operators can potentially cut maintenance costs, reduce carbon emissions associated with machinery, and simultaneously support local farming communities.

Sheep are considered particularly well-suited to this application. Their compact size allows them to move freely beneath panel arrays without causing structural damage, and their grazing naturally enriches the soil through manure, reducing the need for chemical inputs.

For Volkswagen, a company under considerable pressure to demonstrate its environmental credentials following past emissions controversies, the project represents an attempt to diversify its green portfolio beyond electric vehicle production. Partnering with a university also lends the initiative scientific legitimacy, ensuring that data gathered will be peer-reviewed and publicly available.

Poland's rapidly expanding solar sector makes it a fitting location for such a pilot scheme, and the findings could inform policy decisions and commercial strategies across Central Europe.

vocabularyB2.definition: The practice of using the same land for both solar energy production and farming simultaneously
Placing two different activities or systems in the same physical space
Becoming more widely accepted or popular over a period of time
Qualities or achievements that show someone or something is reliable and trustworthy
A small-scale trial project used to test an idea before applying it more widely

articles.questionB2: Given Volkswagen's past emissions controversies, how far can a pilot scheme like this genuinely strengthen the company's environmental credentials, and what risks does such reputational repositioning carry?

articles.title: US soldier killed and one injured after Iranian attack in Iraq
articles.summaryB1: A US soldier has been killed and another injured in an attack in Iraq. This happened just one day after two other American soldiers were killed in Jordan. The US military confirmed both incidents. Iran is believed to be behind the attacks, using groups that support Iran and operate in the region. These groups are sometimes called Iranian-backed militias. The United States has military bases in several countries in the Middle East, including Iraq and Jordan. American soldiers are stationed there to help with security and to fight against terrorist groups. Tensions between the US and Iran have been high for many years. The two countries do not have good relations, and they often disagree about power and influence in the Middle East. When US soldiers are attacked, the American government usually responds strongly. After the deaths in Jordan, US officials said they would take action against those responsible. These recent attacks have put more pressure on the US government to decide how to respond. Many people are worried that the situation could get worse. The loss of American soldiers affects their families deeply. It also affects decisions that political leaders must make about whether to send more troops or to take military action.

Placed in a particular location, especially soldiers at a military base

To react to something, especially by taking action

articles.questionB1: When soldiers are killed in a foreign country, how should their government respond to reduce tensions and protect its troops?
articles.summaryB2: The United States has suffered further casualties in the Middle East, with one soldier killed and another wounded in an Iranian-backed attack in Iraq. The incident occurred just 24 hours after two American soldiers were killed in Jordan, marking a sharp escalation in violence targeting US forces across the region. Washington attributed both attacks to Iran-aligned militant groups, which have grown increasingly active since the outbreak of the Israel-Gaza conflict in October 2023. The US maintains a substantial military presence in Iraq and Jordan, with personnel deployed on counter-terrorism and advisory missions. Iran has long sought to extend its geopolitical influence across the Middle East through proxy forces — armed groups it funds, trains, and directs. Following the deaths in Jordan, senior US officials vowed retaliation, signalling that a military response was imminent. Analysts warn that any such action risks further destabilising an already volatile region. The deaths have intensified pressure on the Biden administration to strike a difficult balance: responding firmly enough to deter future attacks, yet avoiding a wider armed conflict. Critics on both sides of the political aisle argue that US policy in the region lacks a coherent long-term strategy for managing the threat posed by Iranian proxy networks.

vocabularyB2.definition: People who are killed or injured, especially in a war or attack
A situation where something, especially conflict, becomes more serious or intense
Armed groups controlled or supported by a foreign country to fight on its behalf
An action taken to harm someone in return for harm they caused you
Making a country or region less safe, peaceful, or politically secure

articles.questionB2: Given the risks of destabilising an already volatile region, what options does the US realistically have for retaliation without triggering a broader armed conflict with Iran?

articles.title: Norway opens new memorial for victims of 2011 massacre
articles.summaryB1: Norway has opened a new memorial in its capital city, Oslo, to remember the victims of a terrible attack that happened in 2011. The memorial is a piece of public artwork, and it was unveiled on Sunday, just before the 15th anniversary of the tragedy. On 22 July 2011, a far-right extremist killed 77 people in two separate attacks. First, he set off a bomb in Oslo city centre, which damaged government buildings. Then he travelled to the island of Utøya, where he opened fire on young people attending a political youth camp. It remains one of the deadliest attacks in Norwegian history. The new artwork is meant to honour the people who lost their lives that day. Memorials like this help communities to grieve together and make sure that terrible events are not forgotten. They also send a message that society stands against hatred and violence. Norway has worked hard to remember the victims with dignity. The opening of this memorial gives families, survivors, and the whole nation a place to gather, reflect, and pay their respects. As the 15th anniversary approaches, many Norwegians are thinking about what happened and how far their country has come since that painful day.

vocabularyB1.definition: Officially shown to the public for the first time
A date that marks when something happened in a previous year
Something built or created to help people remember a person or event
To feel deep sadness, especially after someone has died
The quality of being treated with respect and seriousness

articles.questionB1: Why do you think memorials are important for communities that want to grieve together after a tragedy?
articles.summaryB2: Norway has inaugurated a new public artwork in Oslo to commemorate the victims of the 22 July 2011 attacks, with the unveiling taking place on Sunday in the lead-up to the 15th anniversary of the atrocity. The assault, carried out by a far-right extremist, claimed 77 lives across two locations: a bomb detonated near government buildings in central Oslo, followed by a mass shooting at a youth political camp on the island of Utøya. The attack remains the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in Norway's modern history. The new memorial forms part of Norway's ongoing effort to honour those who perished while also confronting the ideological hatred that motivated the perpetrator. Public memorials of this kind serve a dual purpose: they offer bereaved families and survivors a dedicated space for reflection, and they function as a collective statement of societal resilience in the face of extremism. The timing of the unveiling, ahead of a landmark anniversary, amplifies its emotional and civic resonance. Norway's handling of the aftermath has drawn international attention over the years, particularly its emphasis on democratic values and measured justice rather than retribution. As the nation marks fifteen years since the tragedy, the memorial stands as both an act of remembrance and a reaffirmation of the values the attack sought to destroy.

articles.title: Russians turn to cash, putting more strain on slowing wartime economy
articles.summaryB1: Russia has been fighting a war against Ukraine for more than four years. This long conflict is causing serious problems for the Russian economy. One big change is that more and more Russians are now using cash instead of paying by card or phone. There are two main reasons for this. First, the Russian government has been cutting off mobile internet in some areas. When people cannot connect to the internet, they cannot use digital payment apps on their phones. Second, many businesses are trying to dodge tax — this means they want to avoid paying money to the government. Paying customers in cash makes it easier to hide income from the authorities. Economists say that when businesses use more cash, the government collects less tax. This puts extra strain on the Russian economy, which is already slowing down because of the war and international sanctions. The shift to cash also makes it harder for the government to track spending and plan its budget. For ordinary Russian citizens, these changes make daily life more difficult and uncertain. The situation shows how a long war can damage not just a country's military, but also its economy and the financial habits of its people.

vocabularyB1.definition: To illegally or dishonestly avoid paying taxes to the government
Extra pressure or difficulty put on something, making it harder to function
The official organisations or people who have power to make rules and decisions
Official penalties or restrictions placed on a country by other countries

articles.questionB1: How do you think the strain of avoiding sanctions and switching to cash might affect ordinary Russian people in their daily lives?
articles.summaryB2: More than four years into Russia's war against Ukraine, the economic toll on ordinary Russians is becoming increasingly visible — not through military headlines, but in their wallets. According to BBC News, Russians have been turning away from digital payments and reverting to cash in growing numbers, a shift driven by two converging pressures. The first is a series of mobile internet shutdowns imposed by authorities, which have left many citizens unable to use smartphone-based payment systems. The second is a surge in tax evasion, as businesses seek to operate off the books and conceal revenue from state oversight. The consequences are far-reaching. When transactions move into the informal economy, the government's tax base erodes, depriving the state of funds at a time when military expenditure is already stretching public finances. Analysts note that Russia's wartime economy has been slowing, weighed down by sanctions, capital flight, and labour shortages caused by mobilisation. The drift toward cash accelerates this deterioration by reducing fiscal transparency and making monetary policy harder to implement effectively. For businesses, cash offers a way to circumvent bureaucratic and financial pressures. For the Kremlin, however, the trend represents a troubling signal: that the economic architecture built around the war effort may be quietly unravelling at its foundations.

articles.questionB2: Given that tax evasion and the shift to cash are eroding Russia's fiscal transparency, what long-term consequences might this have for the Kremlin's ability to sustain its war economy?

articles.title: The European Parliament’s answer to its AI worries: More AI
articles.summaryB1: The European Parliament is starting to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools in its daily work. The institution has decided to allow AI models from four well-known companies: OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, and Mistral. This means that members of parliament and their staff will be able to use these tools officially. But why is this happening now? The reason is that many lawmakers were already using AI on their own, without any official rules. This created a problem, because there was no control over how the technology was being used. By bringing these tools inside the institution, the Parliament hopes to regulate how people use them. In other words, the answer to worries about AI is to bring it under official control. This may sound strange — using more AI to solve problems caused by AI — but the Parliament believes it is better to manage the technology than to ignore it. This is a big step for European politics. The EU has already passed laws about AI, so it makes sense that its own Parliament would try to set a good example. How AI is used inside powerful institutions can affect millions of people across Europe, so finding the right approach really matters.

vocabularyB1.definition: A large, established organisation, such as a government body or parliament

articles.questionB1: Do you think it is a good approach for an institution like the European Parliament to regulate AI by using it officially? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: In a move that might initially seem paradoxical, the European Parliament is responding to its anxieties about artificial intelligence by formally embracing it. The institution is opening access to AI models developed by OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, and Mistral, allowing lawmakers and parliamentary staff to use these tools within an officially sanctioned framework. The driving force behind this decision is a practical one: many members of the European Parliament and their aides were already relying on AI tools independently, outside any institutional oversight. Rather than prohibit a trend it could not realistically suppress, the Parliament has opted to bring usage under formal governance. This strategy reflects a broader pattern seen in organisations grappling with fast-moving technology — acknowledging that a blanket ban risks pushing behaviour underground while offering no accountability. By channelling AI use through approved platforms, the Parliament aims to ensure data protection standards are upheld and that usage remains transparent. The timing carries a certain irony. The EU has positioned itself as the world's leading authority on AI regulation, having passed the landmark AI Act. Yet its own legislature was, until now, largely without internal rules on how members could use the technology. Critics may argue that formalising access accelerates dependency on commercial AI providers, raising questions about institutional autonomy. Supporters, however, contend that transparent, regulated use is far preferable to uncontrolled, ad hoc adoption behind closed doors.
