articles.questionB2: Given that the EU promotes itself as a global leader in AI regulation, does formalising commercial AI access within its own legislature strengthen or undermine its institutional autonomy and accountability?

articles.title: In praise of Scandinavia’s risky and dirty playgrounds
articles.summaryB1: In many countries, playgrounds are designed to be very safe. Equipment is soft, surfaces are smooth, and children rarely get hurt. But in Scandinavia, things are different. Many playgrounds there are built to be a little risky and messy on purpose. Children can climb tall structures, play with real tools, and dig in mud. These are sometimes called 'adventure playgrounds.' Experts say that this kind of play helps children develop important skills. When children face small challenges and risks, they learn how to deal with problems and become more confident. They also get better at understanding their own limits. Some research suggests that children who play in natural, unstructured environments are healthier and happier. In contrast, children who grow up in overly protected environments may struggle more with anxiety later in life. Scandinavian countries have a strong tradition of outdoor play. Many schools and kindergartens encourage children to spend time outside in all weather conditions. Parents in these countries generally trust that a few bumps and bruises are a normal part of childhood. This approach to play is now attracting attention around the world. Other countries are beginning to ask whether their own playgrounds are too safe and whether children need more freedom to explore and take risks.

vocabularyB1.definition: Involving the possibility of danger or something going wrong
Not organised or planned; without fixed rules or a set programme
A feeling of worry or fear that is hard to control
A custom or way of doing things that has existed for a long time
To travel around or try new things in order to discover or learn more

articles.questionB1: Do you think children need risky play to explore their limits, or should playgrounds always be as safe as possible?
articles.summaryB2: Across much of the Western world, playgrounds have been progressively sanitised — rubberised surfaces, rounded edges, and liability-conscious design have become the norm. Scandinavia, however, has largely resisted this trend. In Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, so-called adventure playgrounds give children access to muddy terrain, fire, real tools, and challenging climbing structures, all under loose adult supervision. Proponents argue that this philosophy of managed risk is not negligent but developmentally sound. Child psychologists and educators point to a growing body of evidence suggesting that exposure to minor physical challenges helps children build resilience, sharpen problem-solving abilities, and develop a realistic sense of their own capabilities. Conversely, over-protective environments may inadvertently contribute to rising rates of childhood anxiety and an inability to cope with everyday setbacks. The Scandinavian model is rooted in a broader cultural ethos that values outdoor life — the Norwegian concept of friluftsliv, or 'open-air living,' being perhaps the most well-known expression of this. Schools and early-years settings routinely send children outside regardless of weather, and parents tend to accept that scrapes and bruises are an unremarkable part of growing up. As anxiety among children climbs in many developed nations, this approach is drawing scrutiny from policymakers and educators elsewhere, prompting a re-examination of what safe childhood environments should actually look like.

vocabularyB2.definition: Made excessively clean, safe, or inoffensive, removing anything considered unpleasant or risky
The ability to recover quickly from difficulties or adapt well to challenges

articles.questionB2: Given the evidence that sanitised play environments may inadvertently harm children's resilience, what obstacles might prevent other countries from adopting the Scandinavian model of managed risk?

articles.title: What Britain’s new leader is learning from Donald Trump
articles.summaryB1: Andy Burnham is expected to become the next Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. He has a political style that is very different from traditional British leaders. Burnham loves using social media to talk directly to ordinary people. He often speaks out against snobbish elites — powerful people who look down on others. Many voters feel angry because they believe the government has left them behind, and Burnham says he understands their frustration. His approach reminds many people of Donald Trump in the United States, even though Burnham comes from the political left. Like Trump, Burnham uses strong, simple language and presents himself as someone who fights for forgotten communities. He tries to appeal to working-class voters who feel ignored by mainstream politicians. Some people support his style because they think it gives a voice to those who have been overlooked. Others worry that this kind of angry, us-versus-them politics can divide society. Britain has seen big changes in recent years, including Brexit and growing inequality between rich and poor regions. Burnham, who was previously the Mayor of Greater Manchester, is known for defending the needs of northern England. His rise to national leadership shows how much British politics has changed in recent years.

vocabularyB1.definition: A small group of powerful or wealthy people who have more advantages than others

articles.questionB1: Do you think politicians who appeal to angry voters are good for democracy, or do they make inequality worse?
articles.summaryB2: Andy Burnham, the former Mayor of Greater Manchester, is poised to become Britain's next Prime Minister, bringing with him a populist playbook that has drawn striking comparisons to Donald Trump. Despite occupying the opposite end of the political spectrum, Burnham shares several hallmarks of Trump's electoral strategy: a heavy reliance on social media to bypass traditional media gatekeepers, a rhetoric that frames politics as a battle between ordinary working people and a self-serving, snobbish class of elites, and a deliberate effort to mobilise voters who feel economically and culturally left behind. This disenchantment among working-class and post-industrial communities — particularly in England's north — has reshaped British politics in recent years, most visibly through Brexit. Burnham has long positioned himself as a champion of these neglected regions, and his ascent to national leadership suggests that this outsider posture now carries real political currency. Critics, however, caution that stoking grievance politics, even from a progressive standpoint, risks entrenching division rather than addressing the structural causes of frustration. Supporters counter that without acknowledging the genuine anger felt by marginalised communities, centrist politics will continue to cede ground to the far right. Burnham's challenge will be to channel the disenchantment of forgotten voters into a governing programme that actually delivers, rather than simply performing rebellion against an out-of-touch establishment.

vocabularyB2.definition: Describing a political style that claims to represent ordinary people against a powerful or corrupt elite

articles.questionB2: To what extent does Burnham's populist appeal risk entrenching social divisions, and can a left-wing politician use this strategy without repeating the damaging polarisation seen elsewhere?

articles.title: Greeks ready to pick a fight about ‘The Odyssey’
articles.summaryB1: A new film called 'The Odyssey', directed by famous director Christopher Nolan, has just been released. The movie is based on the ancient Greek poem written by Homer, which tells the story of a hero called Odysseus who travels home after a long war. The film has been very popular around the world, with many people going to cinemas to see it. However, in Greece, the country where the original story comes from, the film has caused a lot of debate. Many Greeks have strong feelings about how their cultural heritage is shown in movies made by foreign directors. Some people are happy that the story is getting attention again, while others are not pleased with the way it has been presented. Homer's poem is one of the oldest and most celebrated works of literature in the world. It has been told and retold for thousands of years. Greeks feel a deep connection to this story because it is part of their national identity. When a Hollywood director makes a film based on such a story, it can spark arguments about who has the right to tell it. This situation shows how ancient stories can still stir strong emotions today.

vocabularyB1.definition: Made available to the public for the first time, such as a film or book

articles.questionB1: When a foreign director makes a film based on another country's celebrated heritage, do you think the people from that country have a right to be upset?
articles.summaryB2: Christopher Nolan's big-budget adaptation of Homer's 'The Odyssey' has generated considerable buzz internationally, drawing audiences to cinemas in strong numbers since its release. Yet the film has also ignited a heated controversy in Greece, the very birthplace of the ancient epic it seeks to bring to life on screen. For Greeks, 'The Odyssey' is far more than a literary classic — it is a cornerstone of national identity, cultural pride, and historical consciousness. The prospect of a Hollywood filmmaker interpreting such a revered text inevitably invites scrutiny from those who regard it as their own ancestral story. Greek audiences and commentators have reportedly expressed mixed reactions, with some welcoming renewed global interest in Homeric tradition, while others have objected to the perceived appropriation of a narrative so deeply embedded in the Greek cultural imagination. The controversy reflects a wider tension that arises whenever Western commercial cinema engages with stories rooted in specific national or ethnic traditions. Nolan, known for his ambitious and intellectually layered filmmaking, brings considerable prestige to the project, which may partially disarm critics concerned about superficial treatment of the source material. Nevertheless, the response in Greece illustrates how ancient texts retain an extraordinary capacity to provoke contemporary debate, particularly when powerful media industries claim ownership — even implicitly — over stories that communities consider their own.

vocabularyB2.definition: Taking something from another culture and using it, often without permission or proper respect

articles.questionB2: To what extent does the commercial appropriation of ancient cultural texts by global film industries risk distorting or undermining the identity of the communities from which those stories originate?

articles.title: Poland commemorate WWII massacres by Ukrainians amid tensions with Kyiv
articles.summaryB1:
Every year on July 11th, Poland remembers the Volhynia massacres. These were terrible killings that happened during World War Two. Ukrainian nationalist fighters killed around 100,000 Polish people in the Volhynia region, which is now part of Ukraine. The killings took place mainly between 1943 and 1945. This date is an official day of remembrance in Poland.

This year, the anniversary is happening at a difficult time. Poland and Ukraine are currently in a diplomatic dispute. The two countries disagree about how to commemorate the victims and how Ukraine should acknowledge what happened. Poland wants Ukraine to formally recognize the massacres as genocide. Ukraine has not fully done this yet.

Poland and Ukraine are both important allies in the region, especially because of the war in Russia. However, history can make their relationship complicated. Many Polish people feel strongly that the victims must be properly honored. They believe this is a matter of national memory and respect.

The ceremony on July 11th brings together politicians, survivors' families, and ordinary citizens. They gather to pay tribute to those who died. The event reminds people that even friendly countries can have difficult shared histories. Finding a way to remember the past while building a strong future together is a challenge that both nations continue to face.

vocabularyB1.definition: The killing of a large number of people, especially in a cruel and violent way
To remember and show respect for an important event or person from the past
An official disagreement between two countries about a particular issue
To officially accept or admit that something is true or real

articles.questionB1: Why do you think it can be difficult for countries to acknowledge painful historical events, and how might this affect diplomatic relations today?
articles.summaryB2:
Poland marked the 81st anniversary of the Volhynia massacres on July 11th, a date designated as the national Day of Remembrance for Poles killed in the eastern borderlands during World War Two. The atrocities, carried out predominantly by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army between 1943 and 1945, claimed an estimated 100,000 Polish lives in what is now western Ukraine. The commemorations this year were overshadowed by an ongoing diplomatic rift between Warsaw and Kyiv, adding a layer of political tension to an already deeply emotional occasion.

At the heart of the dispute lies Poland's long-standing demand that Ukraine formally classify the massacres as genocide, a designation Kyiv has resisted. Ukrainian authorities acknowledge the killings but argue that applying the term genocide could inflame internal political divisions and complicate their own historical narrative around wartime resistance movements.

The timing is particularly delicate given the two countries' interdependence amid Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine. Poland has been one of Kyiv's staunchest supporters, providing military aid, hosting millions of Ukrainian refugees, and advocating for Ukrainian NATO membership. Critics warn that allowing historical grievances to fester risks straining a partnership that both nations need.

Proponents of stronger Polish demands argue that genuine reconciliation cannot be achieved without full accountability. The anniversary thus exposes a recurring tension in post-war European politics: the struggle to reconcile national memory with the pragmatic demands of contemporary alliances.

vocabularyB2.definition: A serious disagreement that damages a relationship between people or countries

Official complaints or feelings of unfairness about something that happened in the past

articles.questionB2: To what extent can genuine reconciliation between Poland and Ukraine be achieved if historical grievances over the Volhynia massacres remain officially unresolved, and what does this suggest about memory in modern alliances?

articles.title: Elon Musk and the age of the corporate leviathan
articles.summaryB1: Some of the world's biggest companies are now so large and powerful that the normal rules for running a business no longer seem to apply to them. Elon Musk is a clear example of this. He controls several huge companies, including Tesla, SpaceX, and X, and has also played a role in United States government through a group called DOGE. This has made many people ask: who is actually in charge of these companies, and who do they answer to? In most businesses, a board of directors is supposed to watch over the chief executive and protect the interests of shareholders. However, at companies like Musk's, this kind of oversight is very weak. Musk has so much personal power that boards cannot easily control him. This situation is not unique to Musk. Other founders of giant tech companies have also built structures that give them almost complete control. The result is a new kind of corporation — one that is so dominant in its industry that it operates almost like a government. Critics worry that when a single person has this much power over a company, ordinary investors and the public can suffer. The article argues that we may be entering a new age where a small number of extremely powerful corporate leaders set rules for everyone else.

vocabularyB1.definition: The process of watching and checking that something is done correctly and fairly.
A group of people elected to manage and control a company on behalf of its owners.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a board of directors can ever truly control a dominant founder like Elon Musk, or is oversight simply impossible in such cases?
articles.summaryB2: A new era of corporate power appears to be taking shape, one in which the world's largest companies operate beyond the reach of conventional governance mechanisms. The Economist's analysis centres on Elon Musk as the most striking embodiment of this trend. Through his simultaneous command of Tesla, SpaceX, X, and his controversial involvement in federal policy via DOGE, Musk has accumulated a degree of personal authority that renders traditional checks and balances largely ceremonial. At most publicly traded firms, shareholders and boards retain the theoretical power to discipline executives. Yet at Musk's enterprises — and at other tech giants built around founder-control structures — accountability has become largely notional. Dual-class share arrangements and cult-of-personality dynamics insulate these leaders from meaningful scrutiny. The article frames this not merely as a story about one individual but as a systemic shift. These so-called corporate leviathans — a term borrowed from Hobbes to describe an all-powerful sovereign entity — have grown so dominant in their respective sectors that they begin to resemble quasi-governmental institutions, setting standards, shaping infrastructure, and influencing public discourse with minimal democratic accountability. Critics argue this concentration of power poses genuine risks to market competition and civil society. Defenders counter that visionary founders create outsized value that justifies their autonomy. What seems clear is that existing regulatory frameworks were not designed for entities of this scale or ambition, leaving policymakers struggling to respond effectively.

vocabularyB2.definition: The systems and rules used to control and oversee how an organisation is run.
The obligation to explain your actions and accept responsibility for their consequences.
A company structure giving founders extra voting power, reducing other shareholders' influence.
Very careful and detailed examination or observation of something or someone.
Describing something that acts similarly to a government but is not officially one.

articles.questionB2: Given that dual-class share arrangements effectively neutralise shareholder accountability, what new governance mechanisms, if any, could realistically constrain the power of corporate leviathans like Musk's empire?

articles.title: How to train for a heatwave
articles.summaryB1: As summers get hotter around the world, scientists are looking at ways to help our bodies cope with extreme heat. One simple method that researchers recommend is heat acclimatisation — a process where you regularly expose your body to high temperatures so that it learns to handle them better. One of the easiest ways to do this is by taking hot baths. Spending time in a hot bath for several days in a row can train your body to sweat more efficiently, keep your heart rate lower in the heat, and cool itself down faster. This is good news because not everyone has access to expensive equipment or specialist training facilities. A hot bath at home can produce similar results to working out in a hot gym. Scientists say that even 30 minutes in a hot bath each day for about ten days can make a real difference. This kind of preparation is especially useful for people who live in cooler climates but travel to hot countries, or for workers who spend time outdoors in summer. As heatwaves become more frequent and more intense due to climate change, learning how to protect our bodies from heat stress could help save lives. Simple habits, it turns out, can be surprisingly powerful tools for survival.

vocabularyB1.definition: The process of getting used to a new or different environment or climate.
To put someone or something in contact with a particular condition or situation.
In a way that works well without wasting time or energy.
Happening often or many times.
Very strong or extreme in degree.

articles.questionB1: Do you think acclimatisation methods like hot baths could become more frequent in everyday health routines? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: With heatwaves intensifying across the globe as a consequence of climate change, researchers are turning their attention to practical strategies for physiological heat adaptation. A growing body of evidence suggests that deliberate heat exposure — most accessibly achieved through hot baths — can trigger meaningful adaptations in the human body, effectively training it to withstand high temperatures with greater resilience. The underlying mechanism involves repeated thermal stress, which prompts the body to increase plasma volume, improve sweat response, and stabilise cardiovascular function under heat load. Remarkably, studies indicate that soaking in a hot bath for approximately 30 minutes daily over a period of around ten days can replicate many of the benefits associated with exercising in hot conditions — without requiring any physical exertion. This has profound implications for public health, particularly for sedentary individuals, the elderly, and those in temperate regions who are unaccustomed to extreme heat but face growing exposure to it. Critics might point out that compliance over ten consecutive days demands a degree of discipline that many people may lack, and that the optimal water temperature and duration still require further investigation. Nevertheless, the simplicity and low cost of this approach make it an appealing complement to broader public health guidance on heatwave preparedness. As extreme weather events become a defining feature of contemporary life, such accessible interventions could prove genuinely life-saving.

vocabularyB2.definition: Relating to the normal functions and processes of a living body.
Strain placed on the body by exposure to very high or low temperatures.
The amount of liquid part of the blood, which helps the body regulate temperature.

The act of following instructions, rules, or a recommended routine consistently.

articles.questionB2: Given the challenges of ensuring compliance with multi-day routines, how realistic is it to expect sedentary or elderly populations to adopt heat acclimatisation practices before a heatwave strikes?

articles.title: Why heatwaves hit women harder
articles.summaryB1:
When the weather gets very hot, most people feel uncomfortable. But new research shows that women are at greater risk from heatwaves than men. Experts are now asking governments and health organisations to pay more attention to this problem and do more to protect women during periods of extreme heat.

There are several reasons why heat affects women differently. Women's bodies regulate temperature in a different way compared to men's bodies. This means women may struggle more to stay cool when temperatures rise. Some women, especially those who are pregnant or going through menopause, face extra health risks during hot weather. Older women who live alone may also be more vulnerable because they have less support around them.

The issue is also connected to social factors. In many parts of the world, women spend more time doing physical work indoors or outdoors without proper protection from the heat. They may also have less access to cool spaces like air-conditioned buildings.

Experts believe that current heat warnings and safety plans do not always take women's specific needs into account. They are calling for targeted efforts to raise awareness and provide better protection. This means creating health advice and emergency plans that recognise the risks women face.

As climate change makes heatwaves more frequent and more intense, understanding who is most at risk becomes even more urgent for public health officials around the world.

The time in a woman's life when her monthly periods permanently stop

articles.questionB1: Why do you think targeted health advice for vulnerable groups like women is often missing from government heat safety plans?
articles.summaryB2:
As climate change drives heatwaves to become more frequent and severe, a growing body of expert opinion is highlighting a troubling disparity: women face disproportionately higher health risks from extreme heat than men. Researchers and health professionals are now calling on governments and public health bodies to move beyond one-size-fits-all heat guidance and instead adopt more gender-sensitive approaches to heat protection.

The physiological differences between male and female bodies play a central role in this disparity. Women's thermoregulation — the body's ability to maintain a stable internal temperature — functions differently, often making it harder for women to cool down efficiently during extreme heat events. Certain life stages amplify these risks considerably. Pregnant women face dangers including premature birth and complications linked to overheating, while those going through menopause may already experience disrupted temperature regulation, leaving them especially exposed.

Beyond biology, socioeconomic factors compound the problem. Women in many regions are more likely to work in poorly ventilated environments or lack reliable access to air conditioning and cool public spaces. Elderly women living alone represent a particularly at-risk demographic, often lacking the social networks that might otherwise prompt timely intervention during a heat emergency.

Despite these well-documented risks, existing heat-health action plans rarely account for gender-specific vulnerabilities. Experts argue that without deliberate, evidence-based policy reforms, women will continue to bear an unfair burden as global temperatures rise. Raising awareness is only a first step; structural change in how societies prepare for and respond to extreme heat is urgently needed.

articles.questionB2: To what extent do you think existing public health systems are structurally equipped to address the disproportionate risks that specific demographic groups face during extreme heat events?

articles.title: Netflix reportedly among parties in talks to buy Letterboxd
articles.summaryB1:
Letterboxd is a popular social platform where people can track the films they watch, write reviews, and follow other movie fans. It was created in New Zealand and has grown to have millions of users around the world. Now, the company may be sold to a large media or entertainment business.

According to an industry newsletter called Puck, several major companies are in talks to buy Letterboxd. These include Netflix, the streaming giant, as well as Sony Pictures and Paramount, which are both well-known film studios. A sale like this has not been confirmed yet, but the reports suggest serious discussions are happening.

For Letterboxd users, a sale could mean big changes. If a company like Netflix acquires the platform, it might use it to promote its own films and series. This could change the independent feel that many users love about the site. Some people worry that the platform could become less neutral if it is owned by a studio that produces its own content.

At the same time, a sale could bring more resources to Letterboxd, helping it grow and improve. The outcome will depend on which company becomes the new owner and what their plans are. Film lovers who use the platform regularly are watching these developments with great interest.

articles.questionB1: If a large studio acquires Letterboxd, do you think the platform will stay neutral for all film fans? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
Letterboxd, the New Zealand-born social network that allows film enthusiasts to log, rate, and review movies, is reportedly in acquisition talks with some of the biggest names in the entertainment industry. According to Puck, a well-regarded industry newsletter, potential buyers include Netflix, Sony Pictures, and Paramount — a constellation of suitors that reflects just how valuable niche, engaged online communities have become to media corporations.

Founded in 2011, Letterboxd has cultivated a devoted, highly active user base that skews towards cinephiles and younger audiences. Its appeal lies partly in its independence from any single studio or distributor, giving it a reputation for authenticity that mainstream platforms often struggle to maintain. The prospect of a takeover by a content-producing giant like Netflix therefore raises questions about editorial integrity and whether the platform's community-driven culture could survive corporate ownership.

From a business perspective, the strategic rationale for such a deal is clear. A buyer like Netflix could use Letterboxd's vast trove of user data and behavioural patterns to refine its recommendation algorithms and better target content at specific audiences. Sony and Paramount, meanwhile, might see ownership as a way to gain visibility for their releases among an already film-literate demographic.

No deal has been confirmed, and negotiations at this stage remain speculative. Nevertheless, the reported interest from multiple major players signals that Letterboxd's cultural cachet has translated into genuine commercial appeal, leaving its passionate community anxious about what any change of ownership might mean for the site they love.

vocabularyB2.definition: The act of buying or taking ownership of a company or asset

articles.title: British couple return to village at heart of deadly Spanish wildfire
articles.summaryB1: A deadly wildfire swept through the Almeria province in southern Spain on Thursday, killing at least 13 people. Among the victims, five are believed to be British nationals. The fire spread very quickly, forcing many residents and tourists to flee their homes and hotels in a hurry. One British couple managed to escape the flames and later returned to their village to see what remained of it. They described the scene as shocking, with many buildings destroyed and the area covered in ash. Wildfires are common in southern Spain during summer, when the weather is hot and dry, and strong winds can help fires travel fast. The Almeria region is popular with foreign residents, especially British people who have retired there. Emergency services worked hard to bring the fire under control, but the dry conditions made this very difficult. Local authorities urged people to follow evacuation orders and not return to dangerous areas too soon. Events like this remind us how destructive wildfires can be, especially for communities in regions with a warm climate. Many families are still waiting for news about missing relatives, and rescue teams continue to search the affected areas.

vocabularyB1.definition: A large, uncontrolled fire that spreads quickly through forests or countryside.
To run away quickly from danger or a bad situation.
The process of moving people away from a dangerous place to safety.
People who live permanently in a particular place or area.
Causing a lot of damage or harm to things or people.

articles.questionB1: If you were a local resident and had to flee your home because of a wildfire, what would be the most difficult part of the experience?
articles.summaryB2: A ferocious wildfire that tore through Spain's Almeria province on Thursday has left at least 13 people dead, with five of the victims tentatively identified as British nationals. The disaster has drawn international attention, partly because Almeria is home to a sizeable expatriate community, many of whom are retirees from the United Kingdom who settled in the region drawn by its warm climate and relatively low cost of living. One British couple, having narrowly escaped the advancing flames, made an emotional return to their village, only to find widespread devastation. Their account paints a harrowing picture of a community grappling with the aftermath of one of the deadliest wildfires to hit the area in recent memory. Spanish emergency services faced formidable challenges in containing the blaze, as persistent drought conditions and strong winds accelerated its spread across the parched terrain. Authorities issued urgent evacuation orders, though compliance was uneven, which may have contributed to the death toll. The tragedy also reignites a recurring debate about wildfire preparedness in southern Europe, where climate patterns have made such events more frequent and more intense. For the affected families — both Spanish and foreign — the immediate priority remains accounting for missing individuals, while questions about long-term rebuilding and the vulnerability of expatriate communities in disaster-prone regions are likely to follow.

articles.questionB2: Given that harrowing events like this reignite debate about wildfire preparedness, what responsibilities do governments have towards expatriate communities living in disaster-prone regions, and how should those responsibilities be balanced with individual choice?

articles.title: US and Iran trade fire as tensions rise over Strait of Hormuz
articles.summaryB1:
The United States and Iran are in a very dangerous conflict. Recently, the US carried out military attacks against Iran. Shortly after, Iran said it had struck US military bases in three countries: Kuwait, Jordan, and Bahrain. These are countries where American soldiers are based in the Middle East.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of water between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. It is one of the most vital shipping routes in the world. Around 20% of the world's oil passes through it every day. If this route is blocked or threatened, oil prices around the world could rise sharply.

Tensions between the US and Iran have been building for many years. The two countries disagree strongly about nuclear weapons, regional power, and support for different military groups in the Middle East.

This latest exchange of attacks is very worrying for global trade and energy supplies. Many countries depend on oil that travels through the Strait of Hormuz. A serious conflict in this region could disrupt supplies and cause economic problems worldwide.

The situation is still developing, and world leaders are watching closely. Many people are calling for both sides to stop the violence before things get worse. The coming days will be very important for peace and stability in the region.

vocabularyB1.definition: A place where soldiers live and work, controlled by an army or government
A feeling of worry and unfriendliness between people or countries that may lead to conflict
A narrow area of water connecting two larger bodies of water
To stop something from continuing normally or working as expected
A situation where things are calm, safe, and not changing in a dangerous way

articles.questionB1: Why might tensions in the Strait of Hormuz disrupt daily life for people in countries far away from the conflict?
articles.summaryB2:
Hostilities between the United States and Iran have escalated dramatically, with both sides exchanging military strikes in a dangerous cycle of retaliation. Within hours of fresh US attacks, Iranian forces claimed to have targeted American military installations in Kuwait, Jordan, and Bahrain — three Gulf states hosting substantial US military presence.

At the heart of international concern lies the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway separating Iran from the Arabian Peninsula. This chokepoint handles approximately one-fifth of the world's daily oil supply, making it one of the most strategically sensitive passages in global trade. Any prolonged confrontation threatening freedom of navigation there could send energy markets into turmoil and destabilise economies worldwide.

The current crisis did not emerge in isolation. US-Iran relations have long been defined by deep mutual mistrust, rooted in disputes over Iran's nuclear programme, its regional ambitions, and its backing of various proxy forces across the Middle East. Each round of strikes risks drawing other regional actors further into the conflict.

For global markets and governments alike, the implications are sobering. Oil-importing nations face potential price shocks, while shipping companies may be forced to reroute vessels at considerable cost. Diplomatic channels appear dangerously strained, and the international community faces mounting pressure to broker a ceasefire before the situation spirals beyond control. Whether either side is willing to de-escalate remains deeply uncertain.

A narrow and critical passage where traffic or trade can easily be blocked or controlled

To reduce the level of conflict or tension between opposing sides
To arrange or negotiate an agreement between two opposing parties

articles.questionB2: Given that both sides appear unwilling to de-escalate, what responsibilities do third-party nations have to broker a ceasefire, and what obstacles might prevent them from doing so effectively?

articles.title: How the biggest trees survive droughts
articles.summaryB1:
Trees are among the largest living things on Earth, but being very tall creates a serious problem: getting water to the top. Water must travel from the roots up through the trunk and branches to the leaves. This journey can be more than 100 metres in a giant tree. During a drought, when there is very little rain, this becomes even harder. Scientists have been studying how the biggest trees manage to survive these dry periods without dying.

Researchers discovered that tall trees use a clever system to move water upward. The water travels through tiny tubes inside the wood. These tubes work a bit like a pump, pulling water up using tension, similar to how a straw works. The tree must keep this system working even when water in the soil is scarce.

One important finding is that the structure of these tubes changes as the tree grows taller. Near the top, the tubes are built differently to handle the extra pressure needed to pull water so high. This adaptation helps the tree cope with dry conditions.

This research matters because climate change is making droughts more frequent and severe. Understanding how trees survive dry periods could help scientists protect forests in the future. Forests store large amounts of carbon, so keeping them healthy is good for the whole planet.

vocabularyB1.definition: A long period of time with very little or no rain
Not enough of something available; hard to find or get
A pulling force that stretches something tight
A change in a living thing that helps it survive in its environment
To deal successfully with something difficult

articles.questionB1: What other adaptations do you think plants or animals might use to cope with drought conditions caused by climate change?
articles.summaryB2:
Standing over 100 metres tall, the world's largest trees face a fundamental engineering challenge: defying gravity to deliver water from soil to canopy. During droughts, when soil moisture plummets, this challenge becomes potentially lethal. A study published in The Economist's science coverage examines the sophisticated internal mechanisms that allow giant trees to endure prolonged dry spells that would kill smaller vegetation.

The answer lies in the vascular system within tree trunks — networks of microscopic tubes called xylem, which transport water upward through hydraulic tension rather than any active pumping. This process, known as cohesion-tension, relies on water molecules clinging together as they are drawn upward by evaporation from leaves. The system is inherently precarious: if air bubbles enter the tubes, they can cause an embolism, blocking water flow entirely and potentially killing branches or the whole tree.

What makes tall trees remarkable is how their xylem architecture adapts with height. Researchers found that tubes near the crown are narrower and more resistant to embolism, compensating for the immense negative pressure required to pull water to such elevations. This structural refinement represents millions of years of evolutionary fine-tuning.

The findings carry real urgency. As climate change intensifies drought frequency and severity across forested regions, understanding the thresholds at which even the mightiest trees succumb to hydraulic failure could inform conservation strategies and help predict which forest ecosystems face the greatest vulnerability in coming decades.

vocabularyB2.definition: The network of tubes inside a plant that carries water and nutrients
A blockage inside a tube caused by an air bubble, stopping liquid from flowing
Uncertain and likely to become dangerous or to fail at any moment
Relating to the movement of water or other liquids through tubes or channels
To fail or die as a result of something overwhelming or difficult to resist

articles.questionB2: Given that the vascular system of tall trees may succumb to hydraulic failure during extreme droughts, how should conservationists prioritise which forest species or regions to protect as climate conditions worsen?

articles.title: Is it true that … we should eat 30 plants a week?
articles.summaryB1: You may have heard that eating 30 different plants a week is good for your health. But where does this idea come from, and is it really true? The claim comes from a large study published in 2018. More than 10,000 people from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia took part. Each person gave a stool sample and reported what they normally ate. Scientists then looked at the microbes, which are tiny living things, found in those samples. They discovered that people who ate more than 30 different plant foods a week had a more diverse gut microbiome. This means they had a wider variety of different microbes living in their digestive system. People who ate fewer than 10 types of plants had less variety. Because of this study, some companies now sell supplements and products that claim to help people reach this goal. However, experts say that 30 is not a magic number. The difference between eating 25 plants and 30 plants a week is probably not very big. Scientists also admit that we still do not fully understand what a truly healthy gut microbiome looks like. So while eating a wide variety of plants is a good habit, you should not worry too much about hitting an exact number.

vocabularyB1.definition: Extremely small living things, like bacteria, that you can only see with a microscope
Containing many different types or kinds of something
The community of tiny living things that live inside your digestive system
Products, often pills or powders, that people take to add nutrients to their diet
A range of different things of the same general type

articles.questionB1: Do you think eating a wide variety of plants is something most people can easily do in their daily lives?
articles.summaryB2: The idea that we should eat 30 different plant foods every week has gained considerable traction in popular health culture, fuelling a growing supplements market eager to capitalise on the claim. But the science behind it is more nuanced than it first appears. The recommendation originates from a 2018 study involving over 10,000 participants across the US, UK, and Australia. Researchers collected stool samples and cross-referenced them with self-reported dietary data, finding that individuals consuming more than 30 varieties of plant food per week tended to have a more diverse gut microbiome than those eating fewer than 10. On the surface, this seems like a compelling argument for hitting a specific target. However, scientists caution against treating 30 as a definitive benchmark. The gap between eating 25 and 30 plants weekly is unlikely to produce any meaningful difference in health outcomes. More tellingly, researchers openly acknowledge that we have yet to establish what an optimal gut microbiome actually looks like, which calls into question the entire premise of targeting a precise number. The study demonstrated a correlation between plant diversity and microbial diversity, but correlation does not establish causation. Meanwhile, commercial interests have been quick to exploit the headline figure, promoting products that may offer little tangible benefit. The broader takeaway is straightforward: eating a wide range of plants is generally beneficial, but obsessing over an arbitrary number may be missing the point entirely.

vocabularyB2.definition: When an idea or movement gains attention and becomes widely accepted or talked about
A standard or reference point used to measure or compare something
A relationship between two things where one tends to change when the other does
A basic idea or assumption that forms the basis of an argument or theory
Based on random choice or personal preference rather than any clear reason or system

articles.questionB2: Given that the study shows only a correlation rather than causation, and that the premise of a fixed benchmark remains scientifically unproven, how should public health advice handle uncertain nutritional evidence?

articles.title: The Guardian view on Homer: The Odyssey is more modern than we might like to think | Editorial
articles.summaryB1: Christopher Nolan, the famous film director, has made a new movie based on Homer's Odyssey, one of the oldest and most loved stories in the world. The Odyssey is about a man called Odysseus who spends ten years trying to get home after a great war. The film will be released soon and many people are excited about it. However, the casting choices have caused a lot of controversy. Elon Musk was angry because the actress Lupita Nyong'o, who is Kenyan-Mexican, was chosen to play Helen of Troy. He claimed this was disrespectful to the original story. Many people disagree and think his reaction shows his own prejudice rather than any real problem with the film. The Odyssey has inspired writers and artists for nearly 3,000 years. The Roman poet Virgil reworked it in his Aeneid. James Joyce moved the story to Dublin in his novel Ulysses. Margaret Atwood wrote a feminist version called the Penelopiad. Each new adaptation brings something fresh to an ancient story. Hollywood is now giving the story its own treatment for the 21st century. The article argues that the universal themes of the Odyssey, such as the struggle to return home, belong to everyone. Great stories can be adapted and reimagined without disrespecting their origins.

vocabularyB1.definition: The process of choosing actors to play roles in a film or play
A situation that causes strong disagreement or argument among many people
A new version of a story changed to fit a different time, place, or format
An unfair opinion about someone based on their race, gender, or background
Thought about or presented in a completely new and creative way

articles.questionB1: Do you think a classic story like the Odyssey can be reimagined with a different cast without losing its original meaning? Why?
articles.summaryB2: Christopher Nolan's cinematic adaptation of Homer's Odyssey is generating intense debate well before its general release. The film has drawn fierce criticism from Elon Musk, who reacted with outrage to the casting of Lupita Nyong'o, a Kenyan-Mexican actress, in the role of Helen of Troy. Musk claimed this amounted to disrespecting Homer's legacy, a position the Guardian editorial dismisses as both incoherent and revealing of the man's own biases rather than any genuine concern for cultural heritage. The editorial frames Musk's intervention as a wearily familiar episode in the endless cycle of online culture wars, where figures present themselves as defenders of western civilisation while making claims that do not withstand scrutiny. At stake is a deeper question about who owns ancient stories and whether their retelling must follow rigid ethnic or racial conventions. Homer's Odyssey, which chronicles Odysseus's ten-year journey home after the Trojan War, has never belonged exclusively to one tradition. Its universal themes of endurance, longing, and identity have made it irresistible to successive generations of artists. Virgil appropriated elements of the story for the Aeneid. Joyce transplanted it to early 20th-century Dublin in Ulysses. Margaret Atwood subverted its male-centred perspective in her Penelopiad. Each reworking demonstrates that great literature gains rather than loses vitality through reinterpretation. Nolan's Hollywood version, whatever its merits, continues a long and legitimate tradition of imaginative engagement with one of humanity's foundational narratives.

vocabularyB2.definition: Unclear and confused, without logical structure or meaning
Careful and detailed examination or investigation of something
Took something from another source and used it for a new purpose
Challenged or undermined an established idea or system in a creative way
Describing something that forms the basic and most essential part of something larger

articles.questionB2: To what extent does Musk's reaction to the casting of Lupita Nyong'o reflect genuine concern for foundational cultural texts, or does it simply reflect the subverted logic of modern culture wars?

articles.title: Why Europe still can’t agree on Israel
articles.summaryB1: European Union foreign ministers met in Brussels to discuss a difficult question: should the EU limit trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank? A growing number of EU countries want the European Commission to propose trade restrictions on goods that come from these settlements. Under international law, these settlements are considered illegal because Israel built them on land that many countries say belongs to the Palestinians. The economic impact of such restrictions would be small because trade with settlements is not very large. However, the political and legal consequences could be much bigger. Countries inside the EU do not agree on this issue. Some support restrictions, while others are against them. This disagreement shows how divided Europe is when it comes to Israel and the Middle East conflict. Critics also say that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has not been tough enough in her response to the situation. The debate is difficult because any decision must follow EU law and satisfy many different governments with different opinions. This story shows that the EU often struggles to speak with one voice on foreign policy matters, especially on very sensitive topics like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

vocabularyB1.definition: Rules that limit or control what people or organisations are allowed to do
Communities built by one group of people on land that another group claims as theirs
The results or effects of an action or decision
When a group of people strongly disagree and cannot reach one shared opinion
Describing a topic that is difficult to discuss because it can upset or offend people

articles.questionB1: The EU is deeply divided on whether to impose restrictions on Israeli settlements — do you think it is easier or harder for groups of countries to agree on sensitive topics than for single governments? Why?
articles.summaryB2: EU foreign ministers convened in Brussels amid mounting pressure from a coalition of member states urging the European Commission to propose trade restrictions targeting goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Although the economic stakes are relatively modest — settlement trade represents a marginal share of overall EU-Israel commerce — the legal and political ramifications are considerably more far-reaching. Analysts Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur argue that the real battle is not about trade volumes but about whether the EU is willing to translate its stated commitment to international law into concrete policy. The bloc's deep internal divisions on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict are once again on display. Member states remain polarised between those advocating firm action and those wary of straining ties with Israel or crossing legal red lines. Adding to the tension, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has drawn sharp criticism from several quarters for what detractors describe as an insufficiently assertive stance on Israeli conduct. The episode exposes a recurring weakness in EU foreign policy: the difficulty of forging a unified position when member states hold fundamentally divergent views. With the conflict in Gaza continuing and humanitarian pressure growing, the gap between the EU's rhetorical commitments and its collective action remains a source of frustration for advocates of a more decisive European response.

vocabularyB2.definition: The complex and far-reaching consequences of a decision or event
Divided into two opposite groups with very different opinions, leaving little middle ground
Confident and direct in expressing opinions or taking action, without being aggressive
Different from each other, moving in opposite directions, used about opinions or approaches
Related to language used for effect or persuasion, sometimes without matching real action

articles.questionB2: Given the EU's deeply polarised member states and the gap between its rhetorical commitments and collective action, what structural or political changes might actually enable the bloc to adopt a more unified foreign policy on conflicts like this?

articles.title: Iranian-born German citizen indicted in Poland for Holocaust denial during Auschwitz tour
articles.summaryB1: A man born in Iran who holds German citizenship has been charged in Poland for denying the Holocaust. The incident happened during a guided tour of the Auschwitz-Birkenau memorial site in southern Poland. During the tour, the man reportedly made comments claiming that the mass murder of Jewish people by the Nazi regime did not happen. Auschwitz was the largest Nazi concentration camp, where more than one million people, mostly Jews, were killed during World War Two. Denying that these crimes took place is illegal in Poland. The man has now been formally indicted, which means prosecutors believe there is enough evidence to take the case to court. If a judge finds him guilty, he could face up to three years in prison. The case has attracted attention because the accused is a foreign national visiting one of the world's most well-known sites of remembrance. Poland takes Holocaust denial very seriously, and laws against it exist to protect the memory of victims. This case reminds us why education about historical atrocities still matters today. It also shows that visiting a memorial site does not always lead to greater respect or understanding of the tragic events that happened there.

vocabularyB1.definition: Officially accused of a crime by police or prosecutors
Formally accused in a legal process, ready to go to court
A place where large numbers of people were imprisoned and often killed
Lawyers whose job is to prove someone is guilty in court
Extremely cruel and shocking acts, usually involving many victims

articles.questionB1: Why do you think some countries have laws against denying atrocities like the Holocaust? Should all countries have such laws?
articles.summaryB2: Polish prosecutors have indicted an Iranian-born German citizen after he allegedly denied the Holocaust while taking part in a guided tour of the Auschwitz-Birkenau memorial site. Auschwitz, located in southern Poland, was the largest Nazi concentration and extermination camp, where over one million people — the vast majority of them Jewish — were systematically murdered during World War Two. The man's comments, made at what is perhaps the most solemn site of Nazi atrocity in the world, reportedly amounted to an outright repudiation of established historical fact. Under Polish law, denying Nazi crimes is a criminal offence punishable by up to three years in prison. If convicted, the accused could face that maximum penalty. The case is notable for several reasons. First, it involves a foreign national, highlighting the extraterritorial reach of Polish legislation on Holocaust denial. Second, it took place at a site that draws over two million visitors annually and functions as a cornerstone of Holocaust commemoration worldwide. Critics of such laws occasionally argue that criminalising speech, even deeply offensive speech, poses a threat to freedom of expression. Supporters, however, contend that Holocaust denial is not mere opinion but a form of incitement that causes direct harm to survivors and their descendants, and that memorial sites deserve particular legal protection. The outcome of the trial is expected to draw international scrutiny.

vocabularyB2.definition: A strong and clear rejection or denial of something, refusing to accept it as true
Relating to laws that apply beyond a country's own borders, affecting foreign nationals
An official act or event to remember and honour people or past events
Speech or action that encourages or provokes others to commit harmful or illegal acts
Very careful and detailed examination or observation of something

articles.questionB2: To what extent should the principle of free expression limit the extraterritorial reach of laws criminalising Holocaust denial, particularly when the speech occurs at a site of commemoration?

articles.title: Can Bending Spoons thrive as a listed company?
articles.summaryB1: Bending Spoons is a software company from Italy. It is unusual because most successful tech companies come from the United States or Asia. The company buys other apps and software products that are not doing well and tries to make them more profitable. For example, it bought Evernote, a popular note-taking app, and made big changes to save money and increase earnings. Bending Spoons uses a strategy similar to private equity firms. These are companies that buy businesses, improve them, and then sell them for a profit. Now, Bending Spoons wants to become a listed company, which means it will sell shares to the public on a stock market. This is a big step for any business. Investors will be able to buy a small part of the company. However, some people wonder if this model can work long-term in a public market. Private equity strategies often focus on cutting costs quickly, but public investors usually want to see steady growth over time. Italy does not have many famous tech companies, so Bending Spoons is seen as a rare success story. Whether it can continue to thrive after listing on the stock market remains an open question. Many people in the business world are watching closely.

vocabularyB1.definition: Making more money than you spend; generating a financial gain.
A plan or method you use to achieve a goal.
A company whose shares are bought and sold on a public stock market.
Small equal parts of a company that people can buy and own.
To grow well and be very successful.

articles.questionB1: Do you think a company can thrive using a strategy of buying struggling businesses and cutting costs? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2:
Bending Spoons, a Milan-based software company, has carved out a distinctive niche in the tech industry by applying a private-equity playbook to consumer apps. Rather than building products from scratch, the company acquires underperforming software assets — most notably Evernote — and subjects them to rigorous cost-cutting and operational restructuring to extract maximum profitability. This model has drawn comparisons to traditional buyout firms, though Bending Spoons operates within the tech sector rather than across industries more broadly.

The company is now preparing for a stock market flotation, a move that would transform it into a publicly traded entity and open its ownership to outside investors. This transition raises substantive questions about whether its acquisition-and-optimisation model is compatible with the expectations of public market investors, who typically prize consistent revenue growth and transparent long-term strategy over short-term margin improvements.

Sceptics argue that the relentless focus on cost reduction may eventually exhaust the pool of viable acquisition targets, leaving the company without a clear path to sustained expansion. Proponents, however, point to Bending Spoons' track record as evidence that disciplined capital allocation can generate durable returns even in a crowded market.

The company also represents something of an anomaly in the European tech sector, where Italian firms have rarely produced globally recognised software businesses. Its forthcoming listing will serve as a litmus test for whether its unconventional approach can satisfy the scrutiny that comes with being a public company.

vocabularyB2.definition: The process of offering a company's shares to the public on a stock market for the first time.
Making major changes to how a company is organised, often to reduce costs or improve performance.
Deciding how a company distributes its money across investments, projects, or acquisitions.
Something that is different from what is normal or expected.
Very careful and detailed examination or observation of something.

articles.questionB2: Given the scrutiny that public markets apply to listed companies, do you think Bending Spoons' acquisition-driven model and focus on restructuring can satisfy long-term investor expectations?

articles.title: How little exercise can you get away with?
articles.summaryB1: Many people think you need to exercise for a long time to stay healthy. But new research suggests that even very short bursts of physical activity can be good for your body. Scientists have found that doing just a few minutes of movement each day can have measurable benefits for your health. This means you do not need to spend hours at the gym to improve your fitness. Even small amounts of activity, like walking quickly for two or three minutes, can make a difference. Researchers looked at data from many people and tracked how their bodies responded to short periods of exercise. The results showed that these brief moments of activity helped reduce the risk of serious health problems, such as heart disease. This is useful news for people who have busy lives and find it hard to set aside time for longer workouts. Experts say that doing something is always better than doing nothing when it comes to physical activity. The idea is that you can get some benefit even from the smallest effort. For people who struggle to stay active, this research gives them a reason to try. Even a short walk or a few minutes of movement every day can help improve your overall health and well-being.

vocabularyB1.definition: Short, sudden periods of activity or energy
Something you can clearly see, count, or prove with numbers
The state of being physically healthy and strong
To make something smaller or less in amount
Sessions of physical exercise, usually planned and repeated

articles.questionB1: Do you think short bursts of exercise could help you improve your fitness in daily life? Why or why not?
articles.summaryB2: For years, public health messaging has promoted the idea that meaningful exercise requires sustained effort — at least thirty minutes of moderate activity, several times a week. New research reported by The Economist challenges this assumption, suggesting that even fleeting bursts of movement carry genuine, quantifiable health benefits. Scientists analysed data from large population studies and found that brief episodes of physical activity — sometimes lasting only a minute or two — were associated with reduced risks of cardiovascular disease and premature death. The findings point to a concept researchers call "vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity," in which incidental movement accumulated throughout the day, rather than structured gym sessions, contributes meaningfully to overall health outcomes. This has particular implications for sedentary populations who struggle to meet conventional exercise guidelines. Rather than framing inactivity as an all-or-nothing failure, the research invites a more graduated understanding of how the body responds to movement. Even climbing stairs, walking briskly between meetings, or standing up regularly may confer protective effects that accumulate over time. Critics caution that such findings should not be used to justify abandoning longer, more structured exercise entirely, as the benefits of sustained activity remain well-documented. Nevertheless, the research offers an encouraging reframing for the millions of adults whose daily routines leave little room for conventional workouts, suggesting that small, consistent efforts are far from futile.

vocabularyB2.definition: Able to be measured or expressed as a number
Spending most of the time sitting down and doing very little physical activity
Stopping and starting at irregular intervals; not continuous
To give or provide something, especially a benefit or advantage
Having no useful result; pointless or unlikely to succeed

articles.questionB2: If even intermittent, incidental movement can confer measurable health benefits, how should governments and employers redesign daily environments to encourage more of it?

articles.title: Hormones on the brain? Everything you need to know about HRT, testosterone, melatonin and more
articles.summaryB1: Many people believe common ideas about hormones that are simply not true. For example, some people think cortisol is always harmful, that testosterone makes people aggressive, or that melatonin is a reliable sleep cure. However, experts say these beliefs are myths. Hormones are chemical messengers in the body. They help control many processes, including growth, mood, and sleep. One common myth is about puberty. Many people think that oestrogen and progesterone only affect girls, and testosterone only affects boys. In fact, all these hormones are active long before puberty begins. According to Sasha Howard, a specialist in children's hormone health at Queen Mary, University of London, these hormones are already working during foetal development, when a baby is growing inside the womb. They are also active in early infancy, during a phase called mini-puberty. This shows that hormones do not simply switch on during teenage years. Understanding how hormones really work matters because wrong ideas can lead people to make poor decisions about their health. For instance, some people take melatonin supplements without understanding what the hormone actually does. Experts want the public to have accurate information about hormones so they can better understand their own bodies. Correcting these myths is a step towards better general health awareness.

vocabularyB1.definition: A false belief that many people think is true
A chemical made in the body that controls how organs and systems work
The process of a baby growing and forming inside the mother's womb
The very early period of a person's life, when they are a baby
A pill or product you take to add something extra to your diet or health routine

articles.questionB1: Which hormone myth surprised you most, and why is it helpful to understand what hormones really do in the body?
articles.summaryB2: A new article from The Guardian challenges a range of widely held misconceptions about hormones, drawing on expert commentary to separate fact from popular fiction. Among the most pervasive myths are the ideas that cortisol is inherently damaging, that testosterone is a straightforward driver of aggression, and that melatonin functions as a simple, dependable sleep aid. Endocrinologists are pushing back against this kind of reductive thinking, arguing that public understanding of hormonal biology remains dangerously superficial. One particularly revealing point concerns the hormones associated with puberty. It is commonly assumed that oestrogen and progesterone belong exclusively to female biology, while testosterone is the domain of male development. This binary view, experts argue, is a distortion. Sasha Howard, a clinical reader and honorary consultant in paediatric endocrinology at Queen Mary, University of London and Barts Health NHS Trust, explains that these hormones are not dormant until adolescence. They are, in fact, active during foetal development in the womb and again in early infancy — a phase Howard refers to as mini-puberty. This early hormonal activity plays a formative role in shaping physiological development well before the teenage years. The practical implications are considerable. Misunderstanding hormones can lead people to misuse supplements or dismiss symptoms that warrant medical attention. By debunking these myths, specialists hope to encourage a more nuanced and evidence-based approach to personal health decisions.

vocabularyB2.definition: A wrong or mistaken idea that people commonly believe to be true
Describing something complex in an oversimplified or incomplete way
The branch of medicine dealing with hormone disorders in children
Temporarily inactive or not functioning, but capable of becoming active later
Showing that a popular belief or claim is false or exaggerated

articles.questionB2: Given how deeply reductive misconceptions about hormones are embedded in popular culture, what responsibilities do medical specialists and journalists share in debunking them effectively?

articles.title: A break from the accommodation mega-sites: the best alternative booking platforms
articles.summaryB1: Most people who book holidays online use big websites like Airbnb and Booking.com. These platforms are popular because they are easy to use and often help travellers find affordable places to stay. However, they are also causing problems in many cities. In places like Barcelona, rents and house prices have gone up because so many apartments are being rented to tourists instead of local people. Barcelona has already banned short-term rentals and plans to ban all tourist apartment rentals by 2028. There have also been reports of tenants illegally subletting their homes on these sites without telling their landlords. Because of these problems, some travellers are now looking for alternatives. A new group of smaller booking platforms has appeared, offering a different kind of accommodation. Instead of large commercial properties, these sites focus on independent B&Bs, home swaps, and private homes that owners actually live in. This means they do not contribute to the second home market. These platforms also try to connect travellers with passionate local hosts who know their area well. By choosing these alternatives, tourists may be able to support local communities rather than harm them. It is a small but growing movement that offers a more responsible way to travel and find a place to stay.

articles.questionB1: Would you choose a smaller, local booking platform over a big site like Airbnb? What makes an affordable place to stay truly good value?
articles.summaryB2: The dominance of accommodation giants Airbnb and Booking.com has long been celebrated for democratising independent travel, but their widespread adoption is now attracting serious scrutiny. In tourism hotspots such as Barcelona — which banned short-term rentals in 2021 and will extend that prohibition to all tourist apartment rentals by late 2028 — these platforms are widely accused of displacing residents by inflating rents and property prices. Adding to the controversy, a wave of headline-grabbing cases has revealed tenants illegally subletting rental properties on these sites without their landlords' knowledge or consent, exposing a troubling gap between platform convenience and regulatory oversight. In response to these shortcomings, a new generation of smaller, independently run booking platforms is emerging as a genuine counterweight to these monoliths. Rather than aggregating vast inventories of commercial listings, these niche sites curate hand-picked properties: owner-run B&Bs, home swap arrangements, and primary residences whose owners are genuinely invested in hosting. The emphasis on passionate, knowledgeable local hosts represents a deliberate departure from the transactional model that defines the market leaders. Advocates argue that using such platforms redirects tourist spending more equitably toward local communities, rather than concentrating profits within large corporations. While these alternatives currently occupy a modest share of the market, they point toward a more community-conscious model of travel — one that attempts to reconcile the freedom of independent exploration with the well-being of the places tourists visit.

articles.questionB2: To what extent can niche booking platforms realistically challenge the monoliths of Airbnb and Booking.com, and what would need to change — in traveller behaviour or regulation — for a more equitably distributed tourism economy to emerge?

articles.title: Nine killed in Russian strikes on Kyiv on eve of Nato summit in Turkey
articles.summaryB1:
Russia attacked the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with air strikes on the night before a major NATO meeting in Turkey. At least nine people were killed and many others were injured. Emergency teams worked quickly to search for survivors under the rubble of damaged buildings. This was the second time in one week that Russia had targeted Kyiv with such attacks.

The NATO summit in Turkey was already a very important diplomatic event, with world leaders planning to discuss the war in Ukraine. The timing of the Russian strikes was seen by many as a deliberate message to those attending the meeting.

Ukraine has been under Russian attack since February 2022. Russia regularly launches air strikes against Ukrainian cities, targeting both military and civilian areas. These attacks cause widespread destruction and put ordinary people in danger.

The international community has condemned the strikes. Many countries that support Ukraine use summits like this one to coordinate their response and decide how much military aid to send.

For Ukrainian citizens, nights like this are a terrifying reality. Air raid sirens warn people to take shelter, but not everyone can reach safety in time. Rescue teams work through the night to pull victims from collapsed buildings.

The attacks remind the world that the conflict continues and that civilians pay the highest price during wartime.

vocabularyB1.definition: Broken pieces of brick and concrete left after a building is destroyed
A person who stays alive after a dangerous or deadly event
An attack on a place using bombs dropped from military aircraft
Done on purpose, not by accident
A safe place that protects people from danger or bad weather

articles.questionB1: Why do you think Russia chose to carry out air strikes on Kyiv just before the NATO summit? Was it deliberate?
articles.summaryB2:
Russia launched a deadly wave of air strikes on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on the eve of a NATO summit convening in Turkey, killing at least nine people and injuring dozens more. Rescue crews worked through the night, sifting through rubble in a desperate effort to locate survivors trapped beneath collapsed buildings. The attack marked the second time within a single week that Kyiv had been subjected to large-scale aerial bombardment.

The timing of the strikes drew immediate international attention, with analysts and officials suggesting the assault was a calculated act of provocation aimed at overshadowing the diplomatic gathering. NATO member states had been expected to use the summit to reaffirm their commitment to Ukraine and potentially announce fresh packages of military assistance.

The strikes inflicted widespread destruction on residential and civilian infrastructure, reinforcing longstanding accusations that Russia systematically disregards international humanitarian law. Ukrainian officials condemned the attack in the strongest possible terms, calling on allies to accelerate the delivery of advanced air defence systems.

From Moscow's perspective, however, military pressure on Ukraine remains a strategic instrument for shaping the terms of any future negotiations. Russia has consistently denied targeting civilians, attributing damage to Ukrainian air defence failures.

For the millions of Ukrainians enduring this prolonged conflict, the strikes served as a grim reminder that diplomatic activity abroad offers little immediate protection against the relentless aerial campaign being waged against their cities.

vocabularyB2.definition: On the day or night just before an important event
An action deliberately intended to make someone angry or cause a reaction
To publicly state again that something is true or that you still support it
International rules designed to limit suffering and protect civilians during armed conflict
